en: Māgha: *Śiśupālavadha* Hari, the abode of the world, dwelling in the house of Vasudeva—the glorious home of the Lord of Śrī—in order to govern the world, beheld descending from the sky the sage born from the body of Hiraṇyagarbha. (MSpv 1.01)
"The movement of the sun is horizontal; the upward flaming of the fire is well known;
yet this radiance falls downward and spreads in all directions—what is this? Thus was it gazed upon by the people with bewildered eyes.
First he was perceived as "a mass," then as "an embodied being" whose form was manifested,
then as "a person" with distinct limbs, and finally, in due order, he was recognized by him as "Nārada."
With his massive clouds hanging lower and lower, white with the pollen of gathered camphor,
he was for a moment clearly comparable to the moon, which is white with the ash of funeral rites and momentarily draped in the skin of a lordly elephant.
His matted locks bore the luster of lotus filaments, while his radiance was like the beams of the autumnal moon;
he was like a great mountain king upon whose lofty peaks grow clusters of snow-plants, as if they were rows of creeping vines.
Wearing a reddish-brown girdle of muñja grass, possessing the luster of a silver-white complexion, and clad in a deer-skin of brilliant sheen, he—
whose lower garment was bound with a golden thread— emulated the form of Śiva, who is clothed in dark-blue raiment.
With its long, golden shoots like the feathers of the king of birds, and its body entwined by the creepers of the golden earth,
it stood tall and white as snow, appearing like a thick cloud at the end of the rainy season with its clusters of lightning.
He shone with a beautiful deerskin rug, its fine hairs naturally variegated and brilliant,
clinging to his limbs as white as a glistening slice of lotus stalk, like Indra’s elephant Airāvata adorned with a richly decorated coverlet.

He shone with a rosary of clear crystal beads that appeared as if its lower half were filled with coral, for it was pierced by the rays from the nails of his thumb— brightened by being struck incessantly against the strings of his lute.
With notes that resounded as they were struck by the wind, each distinct and differentiated within the circles of the musical scales (*śrutimaṇḍala*),
he repeatedly observed the great *mahatī* lute as its specific melodic structures (*grāma*) and modulations (*mūrcchanā*) became clearly manifest.
Having turned back those who followed him after they had prostrated themselves— that treasury of knowledge regarding the sacrifices to the supreme senses—
he ascended to the sky-dwelling abode of the wielder of the discus, which was as beautiful as the peak of Mount Mahendra and where the wealth of the Daityas had been seized.
Before that treasure of asceticism, who resembled a falling sun, could touch the ground in front of him,
Acyuta rose swiftly from his seat with great speed, as high as a mountain peak from which lightning flashes.
Then, as the hosts of serpents below supported him with difficulty by raising and lowering their hoods through great effort,
the two feet of the Son of the Creator were placed upon the surface of the earth by the Son of Devakī.
The First Being (Ādipurusha) duly honored him with the offering of water for the feet and other rites;
for wise men do not come to the homes of those who have not performed meritorious deeds out of their own affection.
The Sage did not seat himself for a long time upon the throne offered by his own hand until he beheld those two men standing there like mountains of snow and collyrium.
Seated upon a throne before the Kaṃsa-destroyer, who possessed the luster of a great sapphire stone,
he surpassed the beauty of the moon as it rose high at evening from the mountain of sunrise.
Having performed the rites of hospitality for him who was well-pleased, the one dear to sacrificers rejoiced exceedingly;
for those of great soul are always intensely desirous of honoring noble men through their service. (MSpv 1.17)
Having placed in his hand a water-pot from which the waters of all sacred fords had been brought and offered by the sages,
Hari, with his head bowed, received those waters which were most efficacious in destroying the flood of sins.
There, by the permission of the Sage, he whose body was as dark as a fresh cloud sat upon that golden throne;
at that moment, that seat surpassed the splendor of the peak of Mount Sumeru, which possesses the beauty born of the Jambū tree.
Clad in garments as radiant as molten gold and possessing the luster of the insignia of a fierce sovereign,
he shone like the ocean embraced by the flames of the submarine fire.
The rays of the sages, mingled with the mass of light from the hand of the Discus-wielder,
shone like the beams of the moon at night passing through the gaps between moving leaves.
With rays resembling full-blown peacock feathers and others as white as the pollen of the *saptacchada* flower,
their stainless complexions were mutually suffused, so that they appeared as if they had become a single color.

In that body of the enemy of Kaiṭabha, within which the worlds rested in full expansion at the time of the dissolution of the eon when his soul was completely withdrawn, the joys arising from the arrival of the ascetics could not find room.
Approaching the sage— who was like the sun at the height of summer, whose radiance blazed forth, and who was blooming with joy—
he clearly became known as "the lotus-eyed one" (Puṇḍarīkākṣa), for his eyes possessed a splendor that rested upon them.

Then Acyuta, making the sage’s body—which was already exceedingly white—appear like a palace by means of the spreading rays of the moon under the guise of the rows of his teeth, spoke these words of pure smiles: *MSpv_1.25*
Your sight removes sin at present, is the cause of future welfare, and has been made possible by past merits;
thus, the sight of you reveals the spiritual fitness of embodied beings throughout all three periods of time.
That unsurpassed darkness which could not be restrained even by the sun— the thousand-rayed one who pervades the world— has been forcibly dispelled by you with your countless splendors.
By the Creator of beings, who acts for the welfare of his subjects and whose mind is undisturbed, you have been made a worthy vessel;
thus, even with constant use, you remain an inexhaustible treasury of the sacred scriptures, like a storehouse of wealth.
O Sage, by this very glance of yours, I have been made one who has fulfilled his purpose, with my sins eradicated;
nevertheless, I am desirous of hearing your most weighty words—for who, indeed, can ever be satiated with that which leads to the highest good?
"Even though he is free from desire, it is by that very [teaching] which compels him to resolve to speak the purpose of his coming—
that your arrival alone, O Teacher, should be bold enough to extend toward us with joyful respect."
To him who was speaking thus, the observer of the vow replied: "O Supreme Person, you must not speak in this manner;
for you alone are to be directly realized—what task could be more weighty even for yogins than this? (MSpv 1.31)

For the wise man who has entered the path to liberation— which is obstructed by surging passion and extremely difficult to traverse because it is not frequently trodden by people— you are the foremost embodiment, providing a refuge free from all danger.

Those who know the ancient truths recognize you as the Primordial Person (Puruṣa), the ancient one who remains indifferent, whose mind is restrained by those who have mastered it, who is grasped somehow through the vision of the inner self, and who is distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti) and free from external modifications.

As the sole architect of the world, you effortlessly established the lofty ground upon the heads of the serpent-lord’s pillars— the very canopy of the world’s single abode, which had been uprooted by the serpent.
O you who have no other teacher, by whom can the singular greatness of your ancient form be comprehended?
Though born as a human, you surpass even the gods and demons through your qualities that bring about the end of worldly existence.
It is said that you descended from the triple heaven intending to lighten this earth, which was fragile under its excessive burden;
yet now that you have supported the three worlds, let the earth be made even heavier by you.

O Lord, if you had not descended to the surface of the earth to utterly overwhelm the world with your own splendor, how could you have become an object of vision for those like me, even when they are fully concentrated? (MSpv 1.37)
O Sustainer of the Universe, you alone are capable of saving this world which is overwhelmed by the intoxication of those arrogant with pride;
for who else but the sun is able to wash away the darkness that stains the night with the sudden impurity of gloom? (MSV 1.38)

O Hari, enemy of the elephants that are the demons led by Hiraṇyākṣa, when people offer praise to you for the slaughter of kings such as Kaṃsa— as if they were merely deer— it is, on the contrary, an insult to you.
I have already begun myself to labor gradually for the purpose of crushing those who hate the world;
nevertheless, my mind, eager for conversation with you, joins me in this through its talkativeness.

O Upendra, let that message sent by Indra—which concerns the welfare of all people—be heard by you for a moment as it is spoken by me; for I have been appointed to the leadership of all affairs on behalf of the Enemy of the Serpents (Indra). (MS 1.41)
There was born to Diti a son of radiant splendor, who was a groundless source of fear for those whose birth serves as an antidote [to his enemies];
him they call the "Golden-cushioned" (Hiraṇyakaśipu) of Hari, the destroyer of the very meaning of the word "Indra."
By that swift Asura, who had long since attained the status of being the primary bearer of the name "Asura" (the envious one),
the gods' minds were struck with a fear such as they had never experienced before.
Since the four guardians of the quarters, having abandoned their respective gods, served him out of passion,
the Goddesses of Fortune (Śrīs) have since then acquired the widespread and disgraceful reputation of being fickle.

Fearing him, the hosts of gods then began by constructing fortified cities, sharpened weapons, powerful heroes, and thick armor— things that for the inhabitants of heaven had previously served only the purpose of enhancing their natural beauty.
To that quarter where he, the refuge of Fortune, wandered through the worlds at will and took up residence,
let the gods offer salutation three times a day with their hands brushing against the jewels of their crowns.
O Nṛsiṃha, as you assumed that lionine body with its thick mane bursting forth in a flash,
he [Hiraṇyakaśipu] countered your tearing of his chest with claws that were curved by contact with the breasts of his innocent beloved.
Then, desiring diversion from the pride born within him, Rāvaṇa— whose name was truly terrifying— again engaged in battle with the gods, a demon who brought ruin to the protection of heaven.
The Lord, desiring to become the master of the three worlds and wishing to sever the tenth head out of excessive passion,
perceived that the grace of the wielder of the Pināka bow— which is consistent with his will— was like an obstacle to the accomplishment of his desired goal.
He who, lifting up the best of mountains, made the payment for the granting of a boon to the wielder of the trident—
the payment consisting of the bliss of being spontaneously embraced by the daughter of the snowy mountain as she trembled in agitation.
"Assault the city! Ravage Nandana! Steal the jewels!
Carry off the celestial nymphs!"—thus did the powerful one, having waged war against the enemy of Namuci, bring constant unrest day and night to heaven.
The graceful gait of the Lord was not like that of a cloud, nor was the wonderful stride of Uccaiḥśravas;
for in battle, the enemy of Bala praised only the swiftness of him who had pursued him.
Unable to endure the sight of him, as one with weak eyes cannot bear the sight of the thousand-rayed sun,
Kauśika entered the interior of a cave-dwelling on the Golden Mountain and spent his days there in fear.

The discus of Viṣṇu, belonging to the Lord of the World, which scatters flickering sparks of fire through its violent friction against the broad and harsh throat of the enemy of the gods, did not overcome his neck.

Like an elephant whose temples are split and who repeatedly becomes turbid with rut, he— having cast aside his gravity and discarded his floral ornaments— did not cause the mind of the Manuṣyadharman (the King) to tremble.
In battles, the serpent-kings, though dispatched by that wise one with wrathful *huṃ* sounds, were turned back;
terrified, they quickly seized the very necks of their attackers like ropes.
By him, the buffalo of the Lord of the Dead had its circle of horns pulled out to serve as a bow;
yet even when that great burden was removed, it carried its head with extreme difficulty due to the weight of shame.
Though he remained at the auspicious hour, full of apprehension,
the Sun adorned his bride with the pearl-like drops of sweat from his forehead caused by his exertion, falling unevenly from the tips of his rays.
The moon did not act as an assistant in his jesting, for it was full of its digits, unwilling to leave its mansion,
and more intent on inciting longing than dispelling the distress of that venomous serpent.
Surely, because this proud man desired to fashion ivory leaf-patterns suited to his clever dalliance, he plucked out one of Ganesha’s tusks; even today, it does not grow back again.

Even though their offense was manifest in the shaking of the garments of women at night, the gods— whose eyes were fixed upon his thighs— trembled with a shudder, being punished by their beloved lord for that faultless transgression.
Slighted by his ever-increasing majesty, which surpassed all people with its great splendor,
the fire within his body bore a canopy of smoke— doubled by tears born of mental anguish.

The serpents did not resort to their natural crookedness; instead, with straight-moving bodies and attentive ears, they abandoned their own defect of double-tonguedness in order to propitiate that blazing fire which was piercing the vital spots of others.

By the elephants of the quarters, whose temples were drenched with rut-fluid as they were struck by his own herds of elephants, who had seized their directions and never turned back, the true nature of their status was finally attained after a long time.
Although his body was already heated by the constant hot breaths of the captive wives of the lord of the gods,
it found no relief from the breezes moistened with water and tender with drops of sandalwood-scented spray.
The six seasons— summer with its heat, autumn, the arrival of winter, and the cold season meeting with the splendor of spring—
assuming the form of flowers, became like resident kinsmen in his city.

Though he knew that one born in the lineage of Manu—non-human, unborn, powerful, and destined to be the end of his own line—had been born, he did not release Jānakī; for those possessed of pride hold their self-respect as their sole wealth.
The son of Daśaratha remembers you as that thief of his wife from the edge of the forest;
having leaped across the ocean, turbid with surging waves, he will slay him near Laṅkā.

Having attained another birth after deceiving his previous one, like an actor assuming a new role, he now appears under the name Śiśupāla; yet even that identity of his is recognized by others as being false.
In his youth, he was four-armed in body, with a face like the full moon and three eyes;
now, as a youth who has forcefully ascended the mountain of kings, he is undoubtedly the sun itself in his splendor.
He himself is the ordainer of favor and restraint for the gods, Daityas, and Rākṣasas according to his will;
he laughs at those such as the Ten-faced Rāvaṇa, whose extraordinary prowess was bestowed by the gods they had propitiated.
Out of the arrogance of his power, that conqueror of the world still exerts himself as before;
for a nature as steadfast as a virtuous woman follows a man even through other existences.
Therefore, O Ordainer, make him—who has transgressed the command of Fate—a guest in the abode of the Consumer of Offerings;
for the wicked, whose misfortunes are ripened by their own evil conduct, must be destroyed by the virtuous.
May the heart of Indra, which has attained firmness through the arising of non-opposition,
once again possess the capacity to endure the pressure of the tight embrace of Pulomajā’s breasts, which are covered in dense horripilation.
When the wielder of the Śārṅga bow had spoken thus, "Om," and the celestial sage had uttered these words and flown up into the sky before him, bearing the splendor of the moon,
the banner of the enraged [Arjuna]— portending the incessant destruction of his enemies— made its abode upon the face of the sky under the guise of a frown directed toward the King of Cedi.
Then, summoned by Pārtha who was desirous of sacrificing,
the enemy of Mura was perplexed by two tasks as he set out toward the King of Cedi.
Then he entered the assembly hall, which was filled with merchants, travelers,
and lords, bearing the splendor of the moon reaching across the sky, accompanied by his heavy poetic compositions.
Blazing forth for the peace of the world,
this triad of human fires arrived and shone brightly upon the altar of the assembly hall.
Reflected in the jeweled pillars,
those images shone as if they were surrounded by attendants, even though they were alone.
Those lofty golden thrones upon which they sat were such that they resembled the peaks of Mount Trikūṭa when it was overrun by the lion Keśarin.
Then, regarding the two teachers and the two duties of both,
the wise one explained that conflict between Hari and the Brahmin.
With smiles whose tips were like jasmine buds, which illuminated the entire assembly,
his pure-toned eloquence seemed as if it had been bathed.
Our words are intended merely to provide an occasion for your speech,
like a prologue for the dramatic plot of a play.
Our son, who has made the kings of the quarters pay tribute through his victorious brothers,
is capable of performing sacrifices even without us, owing to his ascetic power.
One who desires prosperity must not overlook an adversary who is rising;
for the wise have declared that both a disease and such an opponent are alike when they are about to progress.
I do not grieve that the son of the Sātvatī woman has offended me;
rather, it is that he burns the world with pride which causes me such pain.
First, let this opinion of mine be heard, my dear friend;
for even one who has realized the essential truth remains hesitant regarding a matter of action. (MSV 2.12)
Having thus spoken words that were exactly as much as required for the purpose, Mādhava ceased;
for the great-souled are by nature speakers of measured speech.
Then Rāma, throbbing with the lingering resentment of remembering the removal of his rival,
[struck] with his lip, which was skilled in kissing the bimba-fruit-like lips of Rāma’s [wife].

Causing the speech of Pavanavyādhi— which was intended by him and understood by those who knew the meaning, yet had been withdrawn at that very moment— to serve as the position of the respondent (the *uttarapakṣa*).
His two eyes, their reddish luster intensified by the intoxication of tasting wine, rolled about; their sockets were purified by the remnants left from Revatī’s mouth.
He caused his forest garland to wither with the warm breath from his mouth, which bore witness to the hardness of the breasts of women eager for his embrace.
He bore drops of perspiration clinging to his limbs, which were reddened by the heat of his fury, resembling the shimmering stars in a twilight sky flushed with the hue of dawn.
With the luster of ruby petals fixed upon blossoming lotuses,
she created the beauty of a dark upper garment made of fresh sprouts.
Exhaling the fragrance of the mouth-pleasure produced by the wine, which had acquired its scent from dwelling within the interior of the mouth of Kakudmi’s daughter.
With the rays of his prominent teeth, he brought whiteness to the bees that hovered around the lotuses of his face, which served as a mask for his speech.
Whatever was spoken by Vāsudeva— undepressed and free from fault—
the immediate performance of those words was the only reply.
Even though it is brief, this speech does not surpass the more extensive words;
for even the fire that consumes a mass of fuel does not exceed the brilliance of the sun.
Therefore, let there be for us words that are most extensive as an ornament for this very same concise statement, which is so profound in meaning.
The words of the wise render even the lords of speech mute when they utter contradictory words,
yet they make even the dull-witted eloquent when they speak in accordance with the truth.
"Having studied the six qualities, the three powers, and the three arisings of success, even those of dull intellect are capable of explaining them. (MSpv 2.26)
The web of words of a eloquent man who has not investigated his task is in vain;
it is like the flourishes of an archer whose arrow has missed the mark.

Just as for the followers of the Sugata there is no self other than the five aggregates of limbs once all functions of the body have been relinquished, so too for kings there is no mantra other than the fivefold collection of limbs within the body of every undertaking.
A mantra, like a cowardly warrior, cannot remain for long against adversaries, even when all its parts are well-guarded, due to the fear of being betrayed. (MS 2.29)
"Self-advancement and the decline of others—this much is policy. Having accepted this, the wise exert themselves in the mastery of speech. (MSpv 2.30)
Even through supreme majesty, there is no satiety for great-souled beings;
therefore, the great ocean here is seen to desire the rising of the full moon.

I consider that for one who becomes conceited even with very little prosperity, thinking "my success is secure," the Creator has already accomplished his purpose; therefore, they do not increase it further.
Proud men do not rise up against enemies unless they have struck them down root and branch;
in this regard, the sun is the illustrative example, having utterly destroyed the blinding darkness.
Indeed, a firm foundation is difficult to attain without first subduing the opposing factors;
water does not remain still until it has turned dust into mud.
As long as even a single enemy remains, how can there be happiness?
For Rāhu, the son of Siṃhikā, afflicts Soma in the very presence of the gods who slay the Asuras.
An artificial friend is a greater enemy than an artificial foe, for by their actions they may become enemies or friends even when they are natural-born. (MS 2.36)
One should form an alliance with a benefactor even if he is a debtor, and not with a friend who causes harm;
for benefit and injury are the defining characteristics of these two respectively.
O Hari, by abducting Rukmiṇī, you have offended the King of Cedi;
for women are indeed the great root of a tree of enmity that has taken deep root.
When you had gone to the earth to conquer him, he sought to seize this city,
just as darkness seeks to seize the slope of Mount Meru when the sun has departed.
"Enough of this talk, O Babhru; that he abducted his wife is sufficient. For indeed, even the mention of the wicked is enough to bring about misfortune."
"Thus wandering about, he has indeed offended us in many ways;
that son of Śrutaśravas shall be deprived of his life by our ritual action. (MSpv 2.41)
Those who, having established enmity with an angry enemy, remain indifferent,
lie down in the direction of the wind after casting a blazing fire into dry grass.
Or perhaps he may forgive with some slight lack of forbearance, for he is patient; but who could endure being reviled repeatedly through the constant repetition of insults? MSpv_2.43 //
At other times, forbearance is the ornament of a man, just as modesty is for a woman; valor is his ornament in the face of humiliation, just as boldness is during acts of love.
Let there be no birth at all for that person who causes distress to his mother, if he continues to live even while consumed by the suffering of others' contempt.
It is better for a speck of dust, struck by the foot and rising up, to mount upon the head of a living being— even one who is healthy— than for that being to bow down before a god.
For a man who accomplishes no purpose whatsoever through his birth, actions, or qualities,
his birth serves merely as a name, like a word used arbitrarily.
Elevation is not found in the other mountain, nor is depth in the ocean;
O wise woman, both of these are the cause for being unassailable.
Since Svarbhānu swallows the moon quickly while he swallows the sun only after a long time despite their offense being equal, that is clearly the fruit of his gentleness.
When even a slight wind from another approaches and causes him to bow down of his own accord,
a man who is as light as a tuft of grass is the very epitome of those lacking substance.
Among the radiant, the truly radiant one is counted even if he is far away;
the sun is the fifth among the five fires, the source of light.
Without playfully placing his foot upon the lofty heads of his enemies, how could his fame, being without support, ascend to the heavens?
The moon, marked by the deer, was placed upon his shoulder;
he was a lion, a lord of beasts who had ruthlessly driven away the herds of deer.
When an enemy is to be subdued by the fourth means (force), conciliation is a harmful action;
what wise man would sprinkle water upon a fever that requires sweating?
The conciliatory words of him who was filled with wrath, on the contrary, served only to inflame him,
like drops of water upon heated clarified butter.
Those who, through the distortion of virtues,
cause the king's purpose to perish— these are the corruptible ones disguised as ministers, known as enemies.

Some say that one should march when one's own power has increased, while others say it is when the enemy is in distress; however, both of these conditions will rouse you from your current state of inaction.
Your forbearance, O Lord, restrains the Yādava oceans as the shore restrains the sea when it seeks to overflow the worlds— which are themselves unassailable and not small— in its play.

"Let victory be assigned to you as the mere witness of the army, just as the experience of enjoyment is attributed to the self when it is described as the observer of the fruit of that experience. (MSpv 2.59)
When the queen, the daughter of two fathers, had been carried off by the enemy of Hiḍimba in battle,
Sudama, the son of Damaghoṣa, was at long last overcome by his affection for his friend.
That one must resort to another in times of calamity according to policy is a source of shame for the proud;
he is a cause of celebration for him, just as the full moon is to one who has been eclipsed by Rāhu.
One being is unrestrained, while another is constrained by the scriptures;
for how can there be coexistence between light and darkness? (MSV 2.62)
Let Indra’s journey to Indraprastha be undertaken; let the Cedis cease to exist, for in the presence of our elephants, their trees will be reduced to dwarf size.
Let the enemies of the Daśārhas besiege the city of Māhiṣmatī, like cattle blocking a pen when the passage for fodder and the way out have been closed.
"Let the Pāṇḍava sacrifice for heaven; let him enjoy the prosperity of Indra. We shall slay our enemies; everyone strives for their own self-interest. (MSpv 2.65)
May you attain the splendor of lightning through contact with the rays of the sun,
[attained] by means of weapons drenched in blood spurting from the severed heads of enemies.
The words of the agitated Bala were like deities depicted in a painting,
as it were, echoing from the walls of the assembly hall out of fear.
Having heard them, Adhokṣaja signaled with his glance the opportunity for Śeṣa to speak to his disciple, Bṛhat.
Then Uddhava, like Utathya’s younger brother, spoke these words— laden with weight yet free from arrogance—
to the elder brother of Gada before him, in a manner that was truthful.
"It is now improper to speak further once the matter has been determined by the wielder of the mace through his written decree;
indeed, there is no need for oral communication after the message has already been conveyed. (MSV 2.70)
Nevertheless, because you hold me in such high esteem as your teacher,
that very respect becomes the impelling cause for my speaking.
Oh, how infinite is the variety of the world of speech—though composed of only a few phonemes, like musical notes—it possesses a diversity as wondrous as that of song! (MSpv 2.72)
Though one may speak at will and at length on various topics according to one's own desire, a literary composition that maintains a continuous connection of meaning is difficult to produce.
The skillful spread forth their speech, which is exceedingly soft yet dense, fashioned from many virtues, like a variegated cloth.

That the scripture of one who is already a specialist is recited before you is merely a rehearsal of the speaker's qualities; it serves as a cause for the stability of your familiarity [with the subject]. (MSpv 2.75)
A lord should strive to instill wisdom and enthusiasm within himself;
for these two are the root of the self-perfection of one who desires to rise and conquer.
Those wise ones who make their intellect— which is supported by its equipment— a firm bedstead,
and sit upon it incessantly, never know fatigue.
They touch like sharp arrows and penetrate slightly within;
yet even with that which touches much, as it is gross, one remains outside like a ray of light.
The ignorant undertake only small tasks and become easily distracted;
those of cultivated intellect undertake great undertakings and remain undisturbed.
Even for one who employs skillful means, goals perish if he is negligent;
a hunter does not kill deer merely by lying in wait, even though he is prone to his trap.
Not abandoning his radiance even among the twelve kings,
he alone, desiring victory, is like the sun among the Ādityas.
With intellect as his weapon, with the primary elements as his limbs, and a dense cloak of concealment;
with spies for eyes and envoys for mouths—such was that certain king.
For a lord of the earth who knows the proper time, neither brilliance nor forbearance is absolute;
nor is there only vigor or only serenity for a poet who understands aesthetic flavor and emotion.
Even if he has been wronged by others, one who does not manifest agitation remains incurable; or rather, such a person brings about the intended effect for a poet who understands rasa and bhāva.
Tejas, when softened and tempered, is capable of consuming objects;
a lamp takes up its oil by means of the wick situated within it.
The wise man does not cling to finality, nor does he settle for mere human effort;
like a true poet, he regards both word and meaning as a dual unity.
Just as numerous transitory emotions (saṃcāribhāvas) proceed toward the sake of the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva),
so too do many [advisers] attend upon a single sovereign king who is their leader.
Through the application of methods known for weaving threads, she presided over the mandalas,
just as the lords of serpents are easily subdued by a great king.
The tree of energy, with its roots made vast by the power of wisdom, bears fruit when it relies upon the abundant sovereign power that is to be gathered by the hand.
Due to their insignificance or their strength, other kings become the retinue of a king who desires victory, just as other musical notes become the accompaniment of a primary note in a lineage.
Even for the All-pervading One who does not initiate action, objects produced by others become his qualities,
just as sounds become attributes of the sky.
In the garland of those to be attacked, the rear-attacker, and so forth, he who possesses superior splendor acts as the leader,
like a central thread woven through them all for a single purpose.
One should employ the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) according to one's power as an elixir (rasāyana);
in this way, one's limbs become stable and strong. (MSpv 2.93)
It is fitting that those who possess tranquility increase through exertion according to their capacity;
for undertaking an effort beyond one's strength is the primary cause of ruin.
Do not despise him, the lord of the Cedis;
for he is noble and slays his enemies all at once, just as one accents the vowels in a single breath.
Do not think that this king of Cedi is the only one to be conquered;
like pulmonary consumption among diseases, he is the aggregate of all monarchs.
Having achieved his goal through that ally,
he will join with him to break the enemy, just as an arrow fitted with a string is joined to a bow.
And others such as Kālayavana, Śālva, Rukmin, Drumas, and the like—
being of the nature of darkness—
they too followed this corruption.
He sowed dissension among them toward you; though it was slight, it quickly inflamed their anger, just as a small fire, fanned by the wind, consumes heaps of fuel.
Even one who is very small reaches the completion of his task when accompanied by great assistance;
a mountain stream, having joined with a great river, reaches the ocean. (MSV 2.100)
Those kings who are his friends, those who are his enemies, and those who are both—
since they have not been won over by you, they will go beyond you.
"Thus, having raised up the entire assembly of kings for the sake of obstructing the sacrifice, alas!
you have become the first enemy of the one whose enemies are unborn. (MSpv 2.102)
Having recognized you as one whose shoulders are capable of bearing an immense burden, the King of Dharma, together with his kinsmen, desires you as a companion for the yoke of the sacrificial rite.
The high-souled show favor even to their enemies if those enemies seek their protection;
just as rivers and mountain torrents, flowing along, reach the ocean.
Even after a long time, force may succeed against enemies for one who is strong; however, friends who have been alienated are difficult to win back, as they must be persuaded to follow one's will.
"You think that the slayer of enemies is superior for the pleasure of the gods, because he is capable of performing whatever sacrifice is desired for those who consume the sacrificial cake."
That which the virtuous offer into the sacrificial tongues of their mantras is called "nectar" (amṛta);
it is merely a poetic embellishment to describe the ocean as agitated by the churning of Mount Mandara.
"That which was promised by you to your father’s sister, who was waiting for it—'I shall endure a hundred offenses of my son'—that very thing must now be fulfilled. (MSpv 2.108)

The intellect of the wise man is sharp yet not piercing; his action is tranquil yet majestic; his mind is free from malice yet possesses heat; and his speech is singular, though he is a master of eloquence.
Like the sun at the end of a day that it has itself made clear,
even you are not able to bring about his destruction without reaching the limit of the appointed time.
Having established their stations within the sacred fords through secret agents skilled in their duties,
let them discover the depths of the great enemy’s waters.

O King, statecraft that is free from contact with [the sciences] shines like the science of grammar—possessing words placed in accordance with the sūtras, accompanied by good commentaries, and well-composed. MSpv_2.112.

Allies who have entered into a coalition with the enemy should be divided by those who know the enemy's faults, acting as double agents, using manifest commands to incite them while their own faults remain unknown.
The royal attendants, acting as your agents who know the proper means, have reached the city of Ajātaśatru and have become one in purpose with his spies.
While the son of Pāṇḍu was extending his devotion with particular intensity,
those who were fickle became his enemies, for the envious are naturally fickle themselves.
Those kings who here, even while growing up together among those who know the Self, may become like cuckoos with the balipuṣṭa birds;
they will soon be perceived as distinct from him.
May the host of your enemies, arrogant with innate faults and fickleness, and clinging to their wavering and weak factions,
meet the fate of moths in your fire of invincible valor.
Having heard these words of Uddhava’s, which analyzed the matter in this way— acting as a bolt against the path of right method for wicked policy—
he rose up with great joy, his chest uplifted, while the Goddess Śruti sat firmly established upon his breast.
Avoiding the direction of the quarter of Kubera, like a swift arrow released from a bowstring toward the region of Agastya, he—
now gentle, having abandoned his intent for battle— set out for the plateau of Hariharapra-stha.
Even the sun was not fit to touch with its feet him who is worshiped by the world, though those feet are purifiers of the world;
for he bore a parasol as beautiful as the full moon of a great festival.
Standing between two waving chowries as pure as lotus fibers,
he possessed a splendor never before seen, like that of the ocean as the sea of perfected beings (siddhas) falls upon it from all sides.
By the minute, variegated rays of the jewels worn upon their crests,
Govanardhana’s appearance was made to resemble a heap of stones streaked with many minerals.
By the radiance of the emerald gems set at the tips of his shimmering golden earrings,
his chest seemed to have assumed the appearance of a crest of peacock feathers, as was fitting for his childhood.
On their armlets, the two shone forth as they gleamed with a vast canopy of light from the jewels, which had been set ablaze by the friction against the peaks of Mount Mandara.
With the tips of his nails— naturally red, encircled by rings, and streaked with the rays of copper-colored gems—
he shone even now as if drenched in the blood born from the crushing of the chest of the enemy of the gods.
If two separate streams of the waters of the celestial Ganges were to fall from the sky,
they might serve as a comparison for his chest, dark as a tamāla tree and adorned with a string of pearls.
By that water, which was composed of the essence of the ocean and illuminated the quarters with the radiance of jewels,
the world dwelling within it— reflected in his body— was perceived as if manifest before one's eyes.
The pearl necklace, reaching down to his ankles and suspended from the necks of the cranes,
shone like the continuous stream of water from the triple-sourced Ganges as it is spat upward by the big toe.
With a body as dark-blue as a sapphire and clad in saffron-colored garments like camphor,
he shone like a variegated mass of clouds over the sister of Yama, amidst the spreading pollen of lotuses.
"It is only fitting that for this enemy who has been adorned, his splendor became something quite different:
she who is beloved by the entire world was on his whole body, while the other, beloved by no one else, was upon his chest."
Upon his chest, which was as broad and beautiful as a door-panel and where the Goddess Śrī resided like a woman,
there appeared another kind of Lakṣmī who clung to all his limbs and brought joy to all people.

Young women embraced him, whose chest bore the marks of wounds from the claws of the lord of the Daityas— claws that had once been ornaments— which now manifested the qualities of brilliance and hardness upon his breasts.
The upper body of these women seemed to be drawn upward by their breasts, which were exceedingly small yet highly elevated;
meanwhile, their waists, possessing extreme heaviness, bent low as if completely overwhelmed by them.
Whichever timid-eyed woman her beloved gazed upon, she became bashful with her face bent down;
meanwhile, others, free from hesitation and filled with equal jealousy, struck him there with their side-long glances.
With its wheel whose mass of revolving rays had a luster like the flower of the *atasī* plant,
that flood of Yamunā’s water shone like a single arm with a great, throbbing wound.
Skilled in breaking the conflict of adversaries, like the personified power (Śakti) of Hari, she— though occasionally stumbling— was ever present and greatly delighted his heart.
Not only did Nandaka possess a uniqueness belonging solely to Murāri by virtue of being His own property; even by his name alone, he became one who caused extreme agitation among his enemies.

The Śārṅga bow, which has never before been bent by another even when its string reaches the tip of his ear during the act of shooting, remains obedient to him as he stands near you, as steadfast as a true friend.

The Pāñcajanya conch was heard, its deep and resonant sound like that of a swelling thundercloud; it was the lone swan dwelling upon the shores of the dark ocean of Kṛṣṇa, bearing the roar produced by the filling of its interior with the wind of Manodā.

Mounted upon his magnificent chariot, which brought about the fulfillment of his desired goals and followed a path unknown in all directions, that great warrior shone like the lord of the night mounted swiftly upon the Puṣya chariot.
Then the Lord of the Śauris was seen, his form reflected upon the jeweled ground at the tips of the banners,
like the enemy of the serpents (Garuḍa) wishing to speak to the depths of the underworld in order to terrify the hooded snakes.
As he was desirous of departing, the sound of the drum, exceedingly capable of splitting the hollows of the mountains,
drowned out all other sounds, just as the flood of the great ocean drowns out the waters within it.
Since that supporter of the worlds had gone down below to the earth-supporting serpent,
he proceeded with his arms busily occupied by the thousand heads of the serpent, which were bent down by the great weight.
Then the armies of the Lunar dynasty followed him, their banners bent low for fear of breaking against the high arches, like the fruits of action bowing before one who possesses sound policy.
The golden surfaces of the earth were churned by the dark-red ichor of elephants;
along with the masses of chariots whose wheels sank in, they were ground to powder, taking on the luster of the crushed feathers of peacocks.
He did not leap over great men, nor did he ever display arrogance;
he moved as if treading on the dust of the eightfold path, for such is befitting his majesty.
When the Yādavas somehow repeatedly raised their forefeet as they were being restrained,
it was surely because those horses desired to leap over the heavy hands that blocked their path in order to proceed.

The mothers, having come quickly, led their young children away from the roads where they had been playing in the dust, while horsemen, having checked their mounts with effort, looked ahead at the long-stretching line of riders.

Desiring to see him, the throngs of people approached the sinless enemy of Mura from every direction; though he had been praised many times before, he made each person feel as if they were seeing him for the first time, fresh and new at every private encounter.
As he followed the path toward that city, his eyes fixed upon it, the wise man perceived that the chariot was moving slowly, due to the dense, breathless crowds of people. (MSpv 3.32)
In the midst of the ocean, making the quarters golden with the luster of its golden ramparts,
it rose up, cleaving the waters like the flame of the fire that consumes the oblation from the mouths of the beloved wives of the horses.
Having established herself with thousands of mountain rulers and her form encircled by the waters of the ocean,
she was fashioned by the Creator without weariness as a counterpart to the earth itself.
She was the very limit of the expansion of Tvaṣṭṛ’s perfection of knowledge in the arts, acquired through constant practice;
she was like a shadow in the waters of the celestial ocean, visible only upon the stainless surface of a mirror.
The ocean repeatedly fastened garlands of jewels upon the neck of her who was given by her father like a bride to the youthful husband of the chariot’s wheel (Viṣṇu), as she rested there out of love.

By whose rampart—crowded with swarms of conchs tossed up by the mass of waves of the surging ocean—the circle of stars was eclipsed, and Mount Sumeru itself was made to appear like a mere earthen mound. (MSV 3.37)

Where the ocean attained its status as a "treasure-mine" by plundering the jewels— gleaming with the shimmering luster of pearls formed along the merchant routes— which were tossed about by the surging waters that had come there by chance.
The ocean, with its heaps of soft jewels whose luster was veiled by foam,
spread them out upon its surface with its wave-like hands, as if to offer them as a couch for the sun’s heat.
Because of its towering height, the ocean rose up from afar to conquer the Śāla tree;
yet, its desire thwarted by the great waves, it seemed to dissolve as it drew near, as if out of shame.
Out of curiosity, having approached with speed, he was suddenly stopped by the wall of the rampart;
outside that city, the cloud, groaning, wept bitterly under the pretext of a rain of water.
When the Apsarases, desiring some distinguishing quality that would differentiate the form of a woman from the form of a man,
truly propitiated Manu, he created his own offspring marked by the sign of blinking.
Where, having ascended crystal staircases that were obscured by the shimmering nets of moonbeams,
women shone like goddesses traversing the sky during the nights.
There, on the palace rooftops with floors of moonstone as lovely as the moon itself, the channels for the water of the clouds—
even those falling from great heights— carried forth floods of liquid every night.

In that city, during the act of love, the housewives were terrified within their homes by the moonlight reflecting from the walls of cat's-eye gems; they feared it resembled the eyes of a cat, which, though the lamps were visible, were as frightening as those of a wild beast.
Because his palace walls were so exceedingly smooth that they could not be used for painting,
the young men, their own bodies reflected therein, made the jeweled walls appear as if they were living frescoes.

In that city, the splendor of jeweled mirrors was reflected upon the pillars of golden light by the cheeks of women who, possessing a complexion like refined gold, had become pale with love as they gazed at their reflections.
In the verandas of that city, upon door-sills made of parrot-green sapphire and smeared with a luster [of pigment],
the charming women did not even apply the cow-dung marks shaped like a cow's face.
Where the houses shone as if covered by clouds, with clusters of moon-patterns hanging from the rafters that rested for a moment upon them, appearing dark like emerald grass.
It shone with houses that were both vast and peerless, draped with garlands of cloth and yet provided with canopies; which were both variegated and painted, and spacious and abounding in tall trees.

In that city, because of the desire to deceive, people even regarded a cat— sitting motionless upon the pigeon-cotes of the houses amidst rows of artificial birds— as being nothing more than a man-made figure.
Even the women of Kṣitipratiṣṭha eclipsed the moon with their lotus-like faces, while its palaces,
reaching beyond the path of the stars, ascended in vain.

In that city, young men, together with their brides, frequented the balconies which were adorned with beautiful banners and which, being secluded, increased their passion; for these balconies had curved eaves that bent down.
There, the honeyed drinks and the faces of amorous women— each naturally fragrant without prior effort— attained a mutual exchange of their perfuming qualities for the sake of delighting men.
In the intervals between lovemaking, within those houses where flocks of birds had made their nests upon the balconies, turrets,
and gables, the birds— listening to the cries of the women— clearly became their pupils.
Even on those paths that were very clear, where the garments upon the surfaces of women’s breasts— being transparent—
attained a likeness to space not merely in name, but even in actual fact.

In that city, those whose gait was straight, great, free from lameness, and of exceeding length—never stumbling among the people and never deviating even on the two paths—were called "those who follow the disciplined way. (MSV 3.57)
There, the Creator, having fashioned the city women whose peerless beauty rivaled one another,
thoroughly wiped away the stain of the comparison that had been expressed by the single word "equal" regarding the qualities possessed by the goddess Śrī.
The very things that the trees, which grant all desires, bear as fruit are precisely those things that were crushed within his heart;
those riches which had belonged to the people who dwelt there became inaccessible even to his mind.
Possessing every art and illuminating the quarters with the white splendor of his palaces,
he was one whom neither the husband of Revatī nor the lord of Rohiṇī desired to abandon.
There, having encountered Janārdana, whose power as Śambhu had been thwarted in the battle with Bāṇa,
the god of love, Makaradhvaja, dwelt without fear, possessing a victorious arrow in embodied form.
For a long time, she dwelt upon Meru— which was frequented by the auspicious winds, inhabited by Hari,
and which possessed the luster of sprouts of gems with upward-radiating rays— just as Amarāvatī dwells upon the ocean.

He alone, the ornament of the three worlds, surpassed her beauty—she whose face was as if devoid of the luster of its cosmetic paint due to a lack of appetite for black collyrium, even though it was well-applied; he surpassed her as if he were a forehead mark (viśeṣaka) that excels all others.
Beholding that city ahead, he of incomparable prowess reached its gateway—
a splendor like the divine army of the gods, radiant with the brilliance of thunderbolts and weapons, and unassailable by enemies.
Like subjects from the body of the lotus-navelled Viṣṇu, like waters from the slope of Śambhu’s mass of matted hair,
or like the Vedas from the mouth of the Creator, the armies of the enemy of Mura emerged from the city.
With their horses— restless steeds whose bits slipped as they rubbed mouth against mouth—
the horsemen circled with difficulty, their knees pressed painfully against one another.
Even though it was being traversed without interval by throngs of living beings on the long road,
it was rendered unconnected [by them] by means of islands possessing great splendor, like lamps dispelling darkness.

The chariots, falling from their speed, were slowly brought to the ground by horses whose exhaustion was relieved by the tusks of elephants; these steeds, with their necks bent by the long reins held by the diligent charioteers, had their yokes caught upon the tips of those necks.
With the waves of its force, it seemed as if the city's arms—the streets—were being severed at that very moment;
thus, for the most part, it appeared that the supreme Dvāravatī was departing from its state of having the Discus-wielder as its protector.
On the far shore of the ocean, Murāri beheld forest ranges with dark foliage, which,
at every moment, bore the appearance of moss rising up from their banks due to thousands of surging waves.
He gazed for a long time at those who dwelt upon the shore of the ocean— possessing the dark luster of clouds, bearing the marks of royalty,
and accompanied by their creeper-like wives— as if they were his own multiplied selves.
In the vicinity of the ocean, he beheld the lord of rivers, who clings to the earth, roars loudly, possesses great waves with the appearance of tossing banners,
and foams at the mouth like one possessed by epilepsy.

Having drunk from the ocean of waters with excessive greed, he perceived the rays of the moon along the shore as if they were strings of pearls that, though increasing in volume within himself, could not be contained and had thus been cast out.
He saw those clouds drinking the waters from a single region of the ocean— clouds that, roaring incessantly with pride upon the earth, will cause these [beings] to float everywhere.
Having drawn up water from that very source by means of clouds, just as the lords of sages have propounded meaning,
Hari beheld the rivers falling like the Smṛtis descending into the ocean.
Having sold his vast wealth in the various regions, he obtained excellent profits;
then, loading non-perishable goods from those places onto ships, he welcomed the seafaring merchants.
Desirous of rising up by means of the powerful wind of the Lord's loud sighing,
the lords of serpents, out of devotion to the one whose banner is Garuḍa, tossed their waters aloft like banners.
Beholding him who had arrived— the kinsman at the end of an eon— the ocean, resting upon its bed of the lap,
seemed to go out to meet him with its lofty waves extended like arms, out of profound joy.
As he proceeded along the shore, the breeze from the ocean— bearing drops of water in its lap and carrying the fragrance of *melā* creepers crushed by his own wings— cleansed him at every wave.
The marshy regions of the Lāvaṇa and Saindhava coasts were reached by the army’s soldiers— regions where the *ketakī* flowers were parted by the breeze blowing through the dense groves of palm trees.
Adorned with ear-ornaments of clove-garlands and drinking the water from within coconut shells,
they tasted betel nuts and offered their hospitality to him who had arrived from the ocean.

Then, between the army of the younger brother of Bala— which was crowded with hundreds of horses, yet born from a single horse, which had crushed kings at every turn and was itself violently crushed by the Mountain-King (the Himalaya), and which moved forward while constantly maintaining its splendor—

and the ocean— which was crowded with hundreds of waves, yet born from a single horse (Hayaśiras), which had its mountains shattered on every shore and was itself violently churned by the Mountain-King (Mount Mandara), and which moved forward while its splendor had long since vanished— a great difference arose.

He beheld Mount Raivataka, which, like the earth of serpents rising up after piercing through with the luster of its jewels the smoke of their nocturnal breath, possessed various minerals inlaid within its sapphire-blue stones.
With heavy and incessant clouds of dust rising on all sides,
and with canopies of clouds rising higher and higher, it was as if the road of the Lord of Day were once again being blocked by the Vindhya mountains as they rose up.
The mountain, traversed by creepers lovely with dark luster and inviting bees,
was resorted to by those lovely dark stone-creepers which were embraced by bees that had descended upon them.
May Hiraṇyagarbha, who stands pervading the sky with thousands of feet and the earth with his strides, and in whose eyes reside the sun and the moon, be auspicious.
In some places, clouds— pale from the loss of water and possessing a luster like that of a washed upper garment—
appeared as if they were bearing the ashes of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva), scattered by contact with Umā’s limbs.
With its lotus-leaves as umbrellas, it provided shade for the birds— restless with agitation— who, out of intoxication, were somewhat restless and languid like his own fickle and longing wives.
He bore many trees with brilliant blue throats perched upon their trunks,
their bodies entwined by lordly serpents and the tips of their many vine-like branches set in motion, appearing like so many Rudras.

It bore pure waters, white with *śaivāla* moss, which held hanging blue lotuses for ear-ornaments and were as pale as *lodhra* flowers upon their banks, which resembled cheeks adorned with fresh *ulapa* grass.
It bore bees hovering restlessly over rows of lotuses, stealing away the heat with the thickets of its trees;
it was filled with beautiful women whose locks were lovely, and it was protected by Rākṣasas who were themselves unassailable.
The peaks of Sumeru, which were brought by the immortals for the pleasure of Murāri and piled up for him,
cannot render false the qualities of loftiness and beauty of those poets whose speech is unrestrained.

For from that merchant, who was like a wealthy man, the people constantly took immeasurable jewels— of supreme value, filled in vessels not less than a *prastha*, and repeatedly offered in great abundance.
Although the sun, bearing intense heat, was close at hand and held within its rays the lotuses,
the swarm of bees on its bank— having drunk their fill— did not become intoxicated, for they bowed toward the *tāmarasa* flowers.
There, the silver boulder-like rock, by the high tree perched upon it— which possessed a thousand eyes in the form of blossoming flowers—
assumed the grace of an elephant-mate presided over by the Lord of the Gods.

There, the horses of the Sun, shimmering all around with jewels as dark as bamboo shoots, regained their own natural luster through the contact with the elder brother of Garuḍa, who was of variegated hue.

In that forest, the fire arising from the venom of snakes that had not perished did not afflict the trees— trees that were repeatedly drenched by clouds that rose up but did not remain risen for long.
He, by means of his gems which shone like fire due to the touch of the sun’s rays,
proclaimed through the excellence of their receptacle a transmission of qualities that surpassed the original qualities themselves.
Even though that mountain had been seen before, it repeatedly inspired unprecedented wonder in Murāri;
for that very form which attains newness at every moment is the essence of loveliness.

Then, seeing that mountain peak where flocks of birds were crying out as they took flight, and observing that Śauri was standing with his neck upturned, longing to see the mountain, Dāruka spoke thus: MSV IV 18.18: "O you who know how to utter speech, placing your voice upon this mountain which is now raising its wings, look at that mountain peak; seeing him with his neck upraised, Dāruka spoke thus. (Note: The provided Sanskrit fragment appears to be a composite or corrupted version of the verse; the standard critical edition reads: *uccārayan pakṣigaṇās taṭīs tam / utkaṃ dharaṃ draṣṭum avekṣya śaurim utkandharam dāruka ity uvāca //* "Seeing Śauri standing there with his neck upraised, longing to see that mountain peak where flocks of birds were crying out as they flew toward the slopes, Dāruka spoke thus: (MSV IV 18.18)

Who on earth would not be struck with wonder upon beholding this Lord of Mountains, who stands towering over the earth, covering the vast expanse of the quarters with his lofty peaks, established firmly with his high and broad summits, and whose crest causes the rays of the moon to stumble?
When the sun, whose rays extend to the rising and setting mountains, has gone to its setting, and the moon has also departed,
this mountain bears the grace of a lordly elephant encircled by a pair of hanging golden bells.
He who flows all around golden banks, shimmering with green like fresh cloth,
shines like a mountain whose base is composed of yellow orpiment and fresh cloth.
Seated here upon the mountain ridges, they behold the western quarter, where the mass of rays is peaceful and thick with dust;
it resembles the speech of a woman who has attained full satisfaction, and bears the deer resting in its lap—this very form of the moon.
Having made their feet as high as the peaks of Mount Bhṛgu, the torrents of waterfalls, shattered against the mountain crags,
rise up into the sky and cause the bending of the limbs of the women of the celestial world who are afflicted by love.
These clouds, having silenced the cries of the *cātaka* birds with their golden hue, and possessing the brilliance of beautiful gold streaked by lightning, cover the worlds here;
meanwhile, the rays of the sun in certain places turn them a tawny brown, as if shimmering with lovely refined gold.
Supported by the hands of uplifted white moonbeams, with its stars held aloft by towering peaks,
the sky itself clearly falls upon his slopes on all sides under the plausible guise of flowing waterfalls.
In one place, the waters are split by the rays from crystal banks; in another, the water is broken by the luster of blue sapphire stones;
thus, the rivers here partake of the ingenuity of the celestial river (Ganges), assuming the splendor produced by the waters of the Yamunā.
Here and there upon this mountain, the slopes of which possess the splendor of precious gems equal to Meru,
women shine with a fresh passion for their husbands, they who are like the celestial beauties of the gods.
Here, this wall of poor color, adorned with a lofty row of great silver and having the hue of thick white plaster,
attains the grace of the forehead of Śiva, which is whitened by ashes and beautified by his upward-gazing eye.
This [river] bears banks that are exceedingly aged, heavily burdened, obstructed by large, hanging breasts,
constantly difficult to traverse due to their inaccessible nature, and resembling the frontal lobes of elephants in the cardinal directions at the end of an eon.

On the golden slopes, which in color resemble fire, I see trees bearing swarms of bees that have settled upon clusters of flowers; these bees appear darkened as they cling to the blossoms, resembling the form of smoke before the flames.
By this [mountain], which touches the sky and spreads forth walls of gold with the tawny luster of blossoming *campaka* flowers,
the land of Bhārata shines like Ilāvṛta, having attained the beauty of the slopes of Mount Sumeru.
With herds of priyaka deer moving about on all sides, their coats of beautiful and variegated hair shimmering,
she appeared as if she were composed of various jewels that had attained the state of mobility through her limbs.
There, dwelling in the water-basin upon beds of *kuśa* grass, they joyfully sing with voices as sweet as those of young elephants;
and the hosts of *siddhas* likewise sing for the women with voices as sweet as those of young elephants.
When their lord has been overtaken by darkness through the decree of destiny and awaits the time for his departure once more,
these great medicinal herbs here carry him, unvanquished by enemies, as they would a wife in the place of a husband.
Here, the creepers are like young women with hands of tender sprouts resting upon the trunks of forest trees;
or rather, they are like women whose eyes are fixed by swarms of bees, which serve as their flickering glances.

Here, birds, making the air fragrant with kadamba blossoms, perceive the quarters at every moment in many ways; and the wind, shaking the groves of fresh *nīpa* trees, approaches repeatedly, causing the clouds to whirl.
Though it has been explained in some way by scholars devoted to the scriptures, it remains difficult to grasp and uncertain for others;
yet, like a virtuous twice-born man capable of destroying sins, he bears this collection of treasure-mantras with its hidden meanings.
The horse-faced one highly prizes his kiss upon the beloved’s bimba-red lips;
the other, in turn, repeatedly embraces his own wife, whose waist fears being crushed by the weight of her lofty breasts.
This forest which shines along its banks, with its many *tāla* and *tamāla* trees— there,
within the expanse of the forest, no creeper (*latā*) has blossomed that could obstruct the rays of the sun.

In this place, women with large hips, wearing girdles of pure stone and bracelets variegated with fine gems, find a fitting dwelling upon the tablelands where the rocky slopes are smooth and thick with minerals, shining like polished tusks.

Here, this earth, washed with gold, imitates in its entirety the water released by the cloud not long ago, which had long since given rise to the perception of being still, for it is strewn here and there with fragments of diamond.

This woman, whose side-glances are like the arrows of Love, is being attended by many women who entirely avoid contact with people yet intensely contemplate the pleasure of union with their beloveds, and who are themselves bowed down by the heat of distress.
In this place, the female yaks, their minds distressed by the fear of losing a single tuft of hair snagged in the dense groves of kīcaka reeds,
do not venture to move, as if they lack the strength to do so because of the pleasure of hearing the sound from those reed-hollows filled with gentle breezes.
In these ponds, whose depths are hidden by great blue lotus petals, the water— liberated from the clouds like milk white as a pearl—
is swiftly melted by rays dark as a blade, and thus it assumes the clear reflection of indigo-blue water.
She who did not go to her lover as other wives do, whose passion for love was more intense than that of those striving [for it], she—
the woman— is the essence that endures and sustains the longings of those devoted to the passion of love.

When the rays of the moon here have attained the number of a thousand by being split into various high and low beams by the rays of the jewels, the lotus ponds assume the appearance of full-blown red lotuses, as if thinking: "Surely even at night this is indeed the sun, the lord of the earth."

Although it possessed a fragrance that was truly a fit comparison for the faces of women, the blue lotus submerged itself in the surging water as if out of shame, thinking: "Though I have surpassed them, I am now closer [to their faces] because of my distance."

In the lake, the golden ornaments of the women— fallen away as they sportively plunged into the water with impetuosity and turned yellowish-brown by their contact with the *yūthikā* flowers— shone like fragments of the radiance of the submarine fire, *aurvāgni*.

Thinking, "Does this [dust] spread an imperishable luster over the eyes of our young women like a shadow? What need have we for these? the jealous husbands, desiring to conceal their own virtues, thus applied collyrium to their eyes.
When the yellow sandalwood paste had been washed away by floods of water, the necklace— having lost its luster and become pale like the woman herself—
was quickly severed from her two jar-like breasts, as if by a sensitive heart.
Holding no less a quality than nectar, adorned with blooming and shimmering lotuses,
and being enjoyed by lovers together with their beloveds, the lake and the wine both brought about a state of redness in the eyes of the women.
As the women of lovely gaze bathed, their jar-like breasts shone, variegated by large, pure drops of water;
they seemed to have sought refuge on all sides with the gems of their necklaces, as if desiring to become worthy supports for those gems that had slipped from their threads.
Even one's own kin, when fallen from a high position, becomes an object of avoidance for those who are pure;
just as the waters, having cast away the blue lotuses that had fallen from the ears of young women onto the shore by the waves, leave them behind.

The lower lip of the teeth, fresh footprints, unanointed limbs, and the marks of fingernails brought beauty to the women standing in the water; for those who are always dependent on others provide splendor even in times of misfortune.

Upon the face of a certain woman, which bore the design of washed-away leaf-patterns, a variegated beauty was fully spread by the sprouts at the tips of her curls— sprouts that hung down with the weight of water and whose interiors were tawny from contact with filaments.
From the chests of the Yadus, they gathered thick unguents; from their hair, they took away the floral ornaments.
Yet the very lac-dye upon their eyes remained as it was; for indeed, the pleasing sight of the great remains inviolable by others.

The passion that was external was indeed dispelled by water, but that which was in their minds remained exactly as it was; for among the wise, everything that has entered within cannot be overcome by another simply because it is internal.
The play of pearl necklaces upon the foam on their breasts, the beauty of silken garments upon their hips like moss,
and the clear patterns of lotus petals upon their cheeks— these were sufficient ornaments for the women in the water.
The heavy ornaments of the women, having fallen from their bodies into the water, sank as if out of shame;
then they danced upon the discarded wreaths, for even those who are despised become bold when they are exceedingly light.
The tilaka-mark was wiped away, the flower-garlands cast off, the reddish garment discarded, and the body-unguent removed;
thus Kāma, as if full of regret for his pursuit of women, became exceedingly beautiful due to the destruction of his own faction.
As if suffering from the intense affliction of cold due to being sprinkled with water and shaken by a cool breeze,
the new garment clung to the slopes of the breasts of the women, who were possessed of the heat of fresh youth.

Then the groups of beloved women, skilled in the play of shimmering waves, emerged from the lake, their garments’ hems having absorbed an abundance of beauty from contact with their bodies as it dripped like water, even though they were slender.
Seeing her emerging from the water like some celestial Śrī herself, her beautiful hands like shimmering lotuses, and causing even the gods to marvel, Śauri was reminded of the churning of the ocean.
The smooth garment that had been worn by these two for the sake of concealment became stuck to their thighs due to the sprinkling of the *ukā* liquid;
thus, the two most stainless thighs of the women shone forth, as if the silk cloth itself were being hidden by its own radiance.
The women wore garments that surpassed in splendor the radiance of bright clouds, as if out of joy;
