Alas, despite being shaken repeatedly and violently from their bodies, those fresh red garments— having attained an excessive degree of moisture and becoming firmly clung to them— could with great difficulty be separated from the limbs of the lovely-eyed woman.
One woman, her hair disheveled over her shoulders, had been drying for a long time her body still damp from bathing;
but upon seeing her beloved nearby, she did not realize it, and that body became even more drenched with the water of perspiration.

Another woman, her breasts, sides, and armpits visible as she bound her hair-parting with both hands, was repeatedly gazed upon by her husband who longed for her; alas, curiosity never ceases toward those who are dear!
If their limbs are cleansed by bathing in clear water, their lips brightened by the luster of betel,
their garments thin and pure, and if they are not devoid of the flower-arrowed god [Kāma], let such be the extent of the adornment of these radiant women.

Thus, seeing the Yādavas— who had attained an exceeding splendor through bathing in the lake, their stainless limbs radiant, and who were free from envy toward the wives of the city— desiring to behold them, the sun, with its heat, strove even then to plunge into the masses of water of the other great ocean.
Then the sun, as if unable to endure its own intense heat,
descended toward the western mountain in order to enter the waters of the western ocean.
Having gone before him, her face directed toward every window, the woman, filled with intense longing for the pleasure,
repeatedly measured with her gaze the space between the setting mountain and the sun.
With its heat departed, bearing a pale body all around like the crest of a cloud,
the day— its eyes being the sun— having reached its decline and become slack, became exceedingly dull.
As the cool afternoon breeze gently stirred the fingers of the creepers,
the flocks of birds, agitated by fear, uttered cries as if pleading with the trees to grant them shelter.
At that moment, even as the sun was setting, its web of rays remained upon the peaks of the mountain;
indeed, for the virtuous, a state that is truly elevated persists even at the time of their end.
For when fate has turned adverse, even a multitude of means becomes fruitless;
even a thousand rays were not enough to support the sun as it was about to fall.
The moon, having become intensely attached to the quarter of Varuṇa, whose breasts were as red as fresh saffron and who clutched beautiful garments in her hands,
was deeply impassioned by it.
When the sun, possessing the luster of a cluster of *japā* flowers, had gone to its setting,
the circle of the quarters appeared as if its center were bound by a ruby petal of intense redness.
The body of the sun, resembling molten gold, with its form half-submerged in the water,
shone like one of the two halves of the great reed stalk split by the fingernails of Brahmā.

The courtesan of the western quarter banished from the abode of the sky the sun, who, though possessing a body full of passion for her eyes and providing comfort by dispelling heat, was now devoid of his wealth [of light].

The lotus-plant, her lotus-eyes closed as tears of falling swarms of bees flowed from them— tears shed because she was exhausted by long and incessant gazing at the intensely radiant sun with unblinking eyes— closed her eyes.
The sky, with its stars unperceivable, the orb of the moon unseen, and the sun set, shone forth free from heat and devoid of darkness;
for the very absence of faults is the virtue of one who is otherwise flawed.
When their radiant lord had departed for the other world, his exceedingly pure splendors entered the fire;
otherwise, how could that very same husband be so easily found in another birth?
With her hands joined in salutation by the people and bearing the crimson hue of blooming safflower blossoms,
the mother of the Pitṛs did not abandon her natural state, even though she had long since cast off her body as the self-born [Brahmā].
Then, as the two were about to fall, the pair— reddened by the dense rays of the twilight and summoned by the weapon of Hari—
leapt up separately, as if smeared with the blood flowing from hearts shattered by the pain of separation.
"It is well known that this lotus-born [Lakṣmī] has always had her abode here;
yet, at the end of the day, she abandoned even that. Oh, there is no cause for reproach regarding a fickle person! MSpv 9.16.

"The day has gone to its friend, the horizon; alas, why do I remain here without my bracelet?"—thinking thus, as it were, because she had experienced separation from her lord, the light, the twilight also immediately departed.
When the king of birds, the sun, had fallen into the ocean as if provoked by his own reflection,
then the darknesses, dark as a herd of serpents, spread everywhere throughout the world.
The dense darkness, thick with the luster of abundant mud, issued forth from within the mountain caves; having emerged outside, it became even more formidable as it grew intense at the close of day.

Did it hang down from the sky clinging to the heavens, or did it rise up from the surface of the earth? Did it spread out horizontally from the cardinal directions? Thus, as the darkness increased, its origin could not be determined.
When the ground was covered by garments and darkness everywhere blinded the eyes of the people,
the women with beautiful eyes beheld the path to their beloved’s house as if it were a novel ointment of mercury.
Perceiving the gravity of the task at hand, the densest darkness did not cause her fear;
nor did the breasts of the fair-limbed maiden cause trembling in the path of their fine hair-ridge when she approached her beloved.

Even that host of planets which could not be seen by day due to the radiance of the sun, having approached the pervasive darkness of night, seized its light; for the base become manifest by resorting to a dark refuge.
By that convention, unguents, flowers, women provoked by jealousy toward their husbands,
and the flames of lamps simultaneously awakened the long-dormant god of love.
Then, like a mass of light from the thousand gems on the hoods of the Lord of Serpents emerging from beneath the earth,
the shimmering web of rays from the cool-rayed moon adorned the quarter belonging to the month of Madhava.

Enveloped in a clear radiance, his face shone like the form of the moon partially veiled by the mountain of sunrise; with its teeth not yet visible, it appeared as if the eastern quarter were breaking into a playful smile.
With a single digit of the moon before it, the sky— its mass of darkness momentarily thinned and its tresses of hair disheveled—
was for a moment not falsely perceived by the people as the form of Śiva, the Lord of the Gaṇas.

Upon the face of Hari, the crescent moon, captivating the surface of his forehead, appeared like a streak of sandalwood paste upon the dark tresses of Night, which were strewn with blossoms of fresh moonlight.
First it became a digit, then a half, and then the moon, the great cool-rayed one, rose;
surely even those possessed of brilliance do not attain full growth all at once, but rather gradually.
The moon-like face of the daughter of the Naga king, who had first awakened, rose from the bed of the Conqueror of Kaiṭabha with the luster of a white lotus in full bloom, like the cool-rayed moon.
Then the moon-like Dāśarathi, his form as lovely as Lakṣmaṇa’s,
having crossed the ocean and surrounded on all sides by hosts of stars, pierced through the multitude of rākṣasas.
Like a merchant, he constantly subsisted upon the digits of the moon— the lord of the stars—
as it descended into the path of the clouds, assuming a state of complete waning for the sake of the increase of the ocean's waters.
Having reached the night, the moon attained its radiance, and he in turn immediately adorned her;
oh, how marvelous is the mutual action of the great, performed with unhesitating sequence!
Day after day, the moon, touching with his fore-paws the forest of night-lilies— who was as if weeping with her incessant humming and tormented by the rays of the fiercely hot sun— sighed deeply.

Terrified, they beheld her who was like a woman seeking a lover, drenched with the sweat born of passion— like a wooden statue of a moonstone maiden from which drops of water were trickling down due to the rays of the moon, her husband.

The Lord of Herbs, with his rays that dispel all obstacles, acting as a liquid nectar for the lotus-eyed women, thoroughly removed the poison from their bodies—poison that was spreading everywhere and causing intense torment. (MSpv 9.36)
Refracting repeatedly from all sides upon the surfaces of the young women’s cheeks— which were like pure crystal—
the mass of moonlight, which illuminated the quarters of the sky even more intensely, spread forth with great density.

The moon, with its arms of great waves embracing the shores, made even the Lord of the Waters (the Ocean) blind; what wonder is there then that it should so affect the multitude of passionate men, who are lightened by passion? (MSV 9.38)

Lying listlessly within the inner chambers due to his extreme languor, Madana supported himself by grasping the moonbeams as they entered through the lattice windows, shimmering like crystal rods, and rose up.
Surely even Madana, at first, had his range of arrows obscured by darkness;
for it was only when this sun had risen and made the quarters visible that he drew his bow.
When the moon was brought to simultaneous expansion and rising, the swarm of its rays found an opening,
swiftly arriving from the bow of the Flower-Arrowed God, both in the night-lily and in the mind of the woman.
Suddenly illuminating the faces of the quarters and bringing about an intense agitation for the sake of pleasure,
the moon— a second fire born from the eye of Atri— kindled the flower-arrowed god of love.
Thus, certain that their beloveds had arrived with the moonlight, the women began to prepare their toilet;
for at such a time, every preparation is helpful.
They both placed a single necklace as an ornament upon the slopes of their breasts, which were equal in size;
for this very thing, being joined together, fits those who possess such uninterrupted symmetry.
With her thighs as beautiful as the trunk of a plantain tree and her broad hips encircled by a great girdle of many strings, the young woman appeared like the female elephant of the god of love.
The lac-dye on the breasts of the fair-eyed women, the bright lodhra-pollen on their cheeks,
and the fresh collyrium on their lotus-eyes were not distinguished from the milk poured into conch shells.

The women shone with their lotus-like faces, which were blooming on all sides with trembling, radiant lips as petals, with the rays of their teeth as filaments, and with their charming cheeks held like supporting stalks.
Either defeated by his superior excellence, he sought another land, or being skillful, he entered into it;
thus, the moon entered the faces of the fair-eyed women under the guise of reflections in their radiant cheeks.
Surely the arrows of Love have met with a firm resistance upon her great and hard breast,
since they did not cause the slender waist to lose its fullness as they would on other parts of the body.
Even toward things that are delightful, those who possess specialized knowledge do not remain indifferent, thinking, "This is suitable.
When their beloved returns home, the minds of the fair-eyed women are fixed upon garments, ointments, and flowers.
The bride did not smear her body [with unguents] out of fear that it might interfere with the pleasure of his embrace;
for this indeed is quite appropriate for one who is patient—that lack of pride when in union with a beloved.
Another woman, having examined the mouth-perfume with her nostrils, rejoiced slowly as it rose from the hollows of her nose, having been displaced by the surface of her own sprout-like palm.
When the sun and the moon of equal age were held aloft before her, bearing their full-orbed radiance,
the fawn-eyed maidens repeatedly beheld the beauty of their own faces upon the surface of the moon and the mirror.
Placing her arm upon her knee, with the surface of her cheek resting on her bud-like hand pressed in salutation,
she yearned for the lute, which was now devoid of sound as its strings lay slack around her neck.
Then, the most charming young women, skilled in manifesting their affection and exceedingly captivating to the hearts of those they desired,
sent forth their friends toward their beloveds, just as they had previously sent forth their own glances.
"He does not understand my feelings, nor does he realize the compassion I have for him and how he behaves toward me.
Thus, a certain woman, acting as a messenger, gave these instructions to her confidante, saying, "Go and speak to him skillfully."
Though she was urged in haste by her beloved, who was intent on her pride, the friend departed even without being told;
for do not virtuous friends, acting for the sake of their dear ones' welfare, ever require to be prompted? (MSV 9.57)
O friend, if I were to again show compliance toward my beloved after he has committed an offense and broken away from me, then he would surely perceive me as being devoid of self-respect.

Disregarding her beloved, she who was possessed of fortitude then created a conflict with him; for what indeed can be hidden from you? Lacking the restraint of the timid, I am unable to endure doing this.
"Having approached him, do not reproach him; we do not know his fault.
Having reflected thus, the young wife sent her female friend to her lover, even though he had committed an offense.
"Surely, 'send word'—thus addressed by Sudṛśā, she said nothing at all due to her shame;
instead, she gazed intently at her own body, which had been emaciated by the sharp arrows of the bodiless god of love."
The messengers, approaching him with boldness like ordinary men and with words pregnant with meaning, spoke;
for to those of straightforward mind, an action undertaken for the sake of a friend shines beautifully, even if it appears contrary to their natural disposition.
Since he has entered her heart, thinking, "She is the one who stole my beauty and fame on earth," Madana, as if out of envy toward you, truly torments her all the more, devoid of compassion.
When she repeatedly rubs her ear with the tip of her finger during your stories,
it surely increases its density because it remains insatiable, being filled to the brim with the multitude of your virtues.
The juice of the fresh betel leaf, red as a dye, is unable to prevent the lower lip of the dark-lotus-eyed woman from melting away, as it is scorched by her heavy, hot sighs.

Clearly, the arrows of the Lord of Love possess a sharpened edge, since they pierced the hearts of those with eyes like lotus petals, even though those hearts were shielded by the covering of large, firm, and rounded breasts.
"Her body is far more delicate than even a flower"—
this is not otherwise, since the pitiless god of the flowery arrows incessantly and piteously torments her with his own shafts.
"It is true that everything, when improperly treated, turns into poison;
for even these rays of the cold-rayed moon, though they are nectar-dropping, burn her because of her separation from you."
The beloved husband placed his full trust in these affectionate words spoken toward his wife;
for when a person’s inner disposition is already known through their gestures, the words uttered at once find their mark. (MSV 9.69)
First, as if their minds had reached a state of total bewilderment because they were captivated by their beloveds, the youths then set out in pursuit;
once the moon had risen, they immediately regained their footing and followed along the tracks.
From the ear of the dark-browed maiden, who was filled with agitation, there fell a lotus whose bees were humming—
a lotus seemingly driven forth by the expansion of her eyes as they blossomed at the sight of her beloved.
Approaching with sudden haste a certain bride who had risen impetuously— seizing her pair of breasts as if to lift them swiftly toward heaven— he embraced her and held her fast.
As he bore the heavy image of his leader which had followed him body and soul, the mirror—
trembling from the excessive weight— somehow did not fall from the bride’s hand.
As her husband bent down and embraced her tightly, his chest pressed against her two sunken breasts,
the young woman was made to resound with the tinkling of the small bells on her girdle as it shifted at that moment.
As her beloved approached, she rose from her seat without haste;
her garment, which had slipped down so that the hem was tucked up, was then drawn back over her shimmering thigh-walls, which resembled golden slabs seen for a moment.
Approaching him as he was concealing his eyes, people asked, "Tell us, who is this?
The young bride did not answer her beloved with words, but spoke of him through her horripilation.
The body of the beautiful-eyed woman, distressed by her husband’s approach with trembling thighs and violent shivering from shame,
though momentarily bewildered by its own response, nevertheless clearly proclaimed her excessive regard for him.
Though their steps faltered at every stride due to the heavy burden of their full hips as they attended to their husband within the palace,
the women reached the highest pinnacle of affection through those very movements.
The sweet arching of her brows, the graceful movement of her eyes, and her speech, skillful in the application of hand gestures— all these,
though natural to her, became as it were perfected by artistry, manifesting the playful grace of a clear dance for the fair-limbed maiden.
Therefore, my dear friend, it was improper that the Creator did not grant you a thousand eyes;
for by him, the breaker of mountains, the state of Indra has indeed been clearly manifested today in me before the world.
Because you are so close to me, you do not perceive me even though I am constantly before your eyes;
yet how is it that you behold everywhere outside you those who are dear to you, even though they reside within your own heart?
Having thus addressed a certain young woman who wished to depart— her face blooming with a glance cast ahead for a moment—
the youth detained her as her tinkling golden girdle slipped down, released from the grasp of his own hand.

When the deer-eyed woman, filled with anger, cast her eyes askance and turned away in feigned disdain, he stood there in distress even while observing her; for it is said that even the other [the bird] faltered because of that ill omen.
When the proud woman, having beheld her beloved, stood with her hands folded over her garment and her moon-like face bent down,
it was surely because she was gazing upon the foot of Pride as it swiftly made its departure.

The weight of the breasts of Sudṛśā, heated by the fresh offense and quickly embraced by her lover— who was himself burning with the fire of passion— somehow did not cause him pain, even though his own youth was already warm.
Bearing a pair of breasts as cool as Urvaśī, she was like the earth itself descended to the surface (tala) of Urvaśī;
with her incomparable face, she shone with a splendor such that even Menakā paled in comparison to her.
Thus, the rays of the moon were instantly able to unite women with their lovers at will, having quelled the obstacles of jealous anger;
and the *śīdhu* liquors, displaying the playful splendor of the God of Love and skilled in dispelling the hindrance of modesty, acted as teachers in matters of passion for them.
Then the faces of their beloveds— fragrant, captivating to young men, with lotus-eyes brimming with tears of joy— became vessels for wine, as if fashioned from the very essence of life itself.

Then, for a moment, casting aside their pride, those brides offered their embodied forms with respectful service, their discursive thoughts stilled, using words of longing though they were free from desire.
The group of sense faculties was without restraint in that honey which reflected the face of his beloved, which possessed the fragrance of crushed young mango blossoms,
which was delicious, resonant with humming bees, and cool.

Intoxicated and reeling from the fragrance of Kāpiśāyana wine, the six-legged bee settled upon the faces of the women— whose eyes were wide with passion— as if to lie there, mistaking their lotus-like beauty for a drinking cup.

Knowing it to be the reflection of a lotus in a vessel of clarified butter, a bee flew toward the eye of a young woman to smell it; where indeed does discernment exist for one who is possessed by delusion? (MSV 10.5)
The honey offered by her most beloved wife attained a delicious flavor as her husband drank it;
for even though the rays from his golden crown were devoid of consciousness, they seemed to acknowledge their lord.

Through the tasting of the fair-bodied maiden’s lip, the flavor of passion spread here without deliberation; for that very nectar which the youth had previously conceived as something else became, in its taste, something entirely different.
Bearing an exceeding sweetness, the sweet flavor fell simultaneously with their mouths as they blossomed,
and the fragrance of blue lotuses fell with their nostrils.
Desiring to bite her lip, which was like honey in taste and esteemed as a faithful wife,
the young woman’s own self was perceived even by the wind through its deep redness.
For another person, who was intent on drinking the wine from the mouth of his beloved,
the very liquor tasted only once served, on the contrary, as a momentary relish.
Avoided by the faces of the couples— yellowish, cool, smoky, and sweet—
the blue lotus within the goblet sank downward, as if weeping with shame amidst the humming of the bees.

Amidst the threefold intoxication of wit, there proceeded the playful jesting of the fair-browed women, charming with the composition of their artful speech and accompanied by laughter that revealed hidden secrets.
Coquettish smiles, eloquence in speech, and particular transformations in the gaze were produced intensely in the bride, though she was naturally modest, by intoxication as if by a young lover.
The hearts of the young wives— unpleasant toward their offending husbands, blazing with anger, and having summoned fortitude—
were as if washed clean, as if pacified, or as if melted away by the streams of honey-wine.

The intoxication of wine brought forth the latent delusion in the limbs of the young women— delusion that was already present but remained unmanifest due to long-standing habit, just as a prefix reveals a meaning hidden within a verbal root.
Their speech was left unfinished, their indifference was shown toward their withered garlands, garments, and ornaments;
and their rising up to depart without apparent cause revealed the intoxication and amorous confusion of those women.
With her eyes half-closed, their lashes slightly parted, and her modesty melting away under the influence of wine,
the young bride gazed slowly at the face of her lover while keeping her own head bowed down.

She who had previously dared to speak to her beloved in some way through the words of a friend, now fell into a stupor of shame upon drinking wine; for everyone returns to their natural state once the intoxication has passed.
The inner passion of the woman toward her beloved, which had long been somehow concealed by shame,
then became manifest through her eyes, as if it were the very redness [of intoxication] arising from the fearlessness brought on by the wine.
When their beloveds had returned from countless journeys and were desirous of reconciling with them,
the opportunity for wine arose in the hearts of the fair-browed women, which were now filled with regret.

"O woman, do not again pursue him who has committed an offense against you, your mind deluded by intoxication! Do not desire liquor; indeed, pride is harder to abandon than even pleasure. (MSpv 10.21)
He led them into the presence of those who had utterly destroyed shame and delusion for the sake of the pleasure of love;
the honey they consumed immediately bore fruit, as if it were imbued with serenity.

The wine offered by their lovers, infused with intoxicants and permeated with an abundance of savory juices, caused the women to thrill; thus, while the name "wine" (sura) was already established, its true meaning was now fully realized.

The fragrance of the wine, having acquired the quality of perfume, and the scent of the goblet from the woman’s mouth— through their mutual union, the delighting bees attained a state of excellence that seemed almost transcendent.

By means of its clever artifice in breaking their pride, by generating a desire for amorous play, by spreading passion in their gaze, and by cultivating emotion within them, intoxication suddenly took hold of the women, as if it were a lover.
O Upali, those fair-browed women, skilled in secret kissing,
stained their own lips with the essence of the lip-rouge of their lovers, which had been washed away by drinking.

Although she had tasted the wine offered by her lover while he called out the name of another young woman, she cast off her pride; yet the other woman, though not drinking, became intoxicated upon seeing it.

Though she had drunk much wine, she could not find satisfaction; for how can joy be the cause of intoxication for one whose mind is despondent, having become suspicious of her lord of the heart, whose thoughts were fixed on another woman?
Having previously refused his conciliatory words out of anger, and now with her delusion intensified by the intoxication of wine,
she— her heart distressed by the thought of separation— perceived her lover as one who had provoked her and thus sought to appease him.
As their eyes were half-closed and their limbs grew languid,
intoxication itself— seizing their modesty as if out of envy— took upon itself the very qualities of those women.
Formerly, the reflection of the moon appeared upon the cheeks of those with unanointed eyes, which were as smooth as temple walls;
later, when their luster was ruddy from drinking, it took on the form of a tilaka mark made of lodhra powder.
As if tossed by the mutual impact of their jar-like breasts on both sides,
the bodies of the women, intoxicated with excessive passion, reeled about like men possessed of extreme infatuation.

Beauty adorned their bodies; the union with full and fresh youth adorned that beauty; in turn, the fortune of being the mark of the god whose banner is the makara adorned that youth; and intoxication, adorned by union with a beloved, adorned that fortune.

While they were constantly falling into intoxication, alternating between anger and delight, the Bodhisattva did not take up his bow with its arrow, nor did he cast aside his discarded quiver; for he was no longer the god of love.
The beloved was clearly recognized by the other women with their own wives;
for a mind whose conventional veil is destroyed by envy is not capable of investigating the truth.
Their faces blossomed with joy toward their beloveds; their bodies became thrilled;
their hearts attained a state of melting tenderness, and their anger flickered within their words.

Their form was unassailable and charming; their affection blossomed regardless of what ought to be done; and their flirtations were free from artificiality or agitation—these qualities became a magical spell over their lovers. (MSV 10.37)
Having effortlessly outbalanced even his profound gravity with her playful charm,
that merchant of beauty— her face, which knows how to humble pride— has already purchased the heart of her beloved.
Upon the beloved and upon the couch— both possessing smooth, fair skin and fashioned for the pleasure of the deer-eyed women— their glances fell incessantly, bowing down in devotion.

Although the eyes of the young women were tremulous with passion and cast oblique glances, those far-sighted maidens did not transgress the ear— the organ endowed with the virtue of hearing— of the youth.
Desiring to converse, she was unable to speak; though wishing to look at him, she could not face him directly;
and though her limbs were restless with longing, the lady with the arched brows trembled at the touch of her beloved.
Another woman, her sense of modesty constrained by the rules of decorum regarding her upper garment, seemed to block the path of his gaze;
yet another, with her breasts pressed against the broad chest of her husband, acted as a barrier.
As her garment was being snatched away by her husband, she— whose lovely breasts were concealed by the crossed position of her slender arms and whose conch-shell bracelets were shattered—
impetuously embraced her newly wed bridegroom.

The Lord of Rati suddenly withdrew his great arrows from the young men, who had abandoned their hostility toward those embracing their beloveds; the arrows, which had been aimed, now had their anger dissolved by smiles.
As the garment was slipping away from the bride, she, having embraced him, drew it back with passion; like a skillful woman, she held fast the cloth clinging to her own hips with her own body.

Having gazed for a moment at the eyes of the women, which resembled those of a doe,
the deer then fled in terror, their movements distorted by various signs of agitation.
Having been led down from the low ground by their riders with effort, the herds of horses, their reins loosened, slowly emerged from the depths;
then, galloping swiftly, they raised a loud clamor from their high-stepping hooves.
By some man who had just mounted the road and was waiting for people,
skill was indeed rewarded with immediate fruit, as that young slave-boy devoured the forest thickets right before him.

The army of Śauri, with its many parasols due to the multitude of kings who had submitted to his majesty and arrived from here and there with bodies bowed in humility, became one under a single umbrella.
Hearing the sound of the two bells of the elephant following behind as it approached, the women became agitated;
the soldiers quickly moved aside from the road, setting down their heavy loads at a distance.

In the presence of Upendra, the bards recited many verses, pointing out his virtues— those who were full of vigor, radiant with complexion, endowed with noble conduct, gracious, and who had not abandoned the awareness of their lineage.
Even the ocean, though moving and its waters having completely overspread the earth, maintains its stability;
yet what lawlessness did Keśava not cause even while on the move, through his unrestrained armies in the villages?
With faces possessing the luster of clusters of *kośātakī* flowers and eyes wide open like fierce arrows,
the village women, unobserved by the people, gazed for a long time upon those who were dead.

In the cow-pens, he saw the villagers— seated in circles for social gatherings, rising repeatedly with loud cries, and leaping about as they thirsted for the brown soma— whose minds were stirred by the chanting of their own ancestral lineages.

Even though they had already achieved their purpose, the cowherd folk could not reach satiety as they gazed upon the Lord of Men with eyes whose wide-reaching qualities were well-known, yet whose bewilderment remained unperceived due to their singular innocence.

Holding the calves with both knees and licking them out of affection, he watched for a long time as the cowherds milked the cows— whose udders were swelling like rising streams— while they held the ropes with both hands.
As he approached, his calves moving with great speed, extending his hand to lead the herd forward and desiring to milk it from the group of cows,
his enemy beheld that preeminent cow of the herd as she emerged from the flock, her lowing beautiful with the sound "hum."
While he went as far as the rice fields to gather parrots,
he beheld with a smile the agitated cowherd women on all sides of the fields, whose beauty was being ravaged by deer.
Hearing the songs of the cowherd girls, Hari looked out, thinking: "The deer herd is surely not eating the young grass, for the sun is about to move away from us due to our lack of vigilance."
The soft sound of the tinkling anklets of women moving playfully— resembling red lotuses at their feet—
captivated the minds of those near the shore, surpassing the cries of intoxicated cranes from within the water.

As he proceeded from afar, some kings received with their heads the dense mass of dust raised by his army— a cloud that had risen high, was unbroken, and was exceedingly heavy— while others received his command.
Generally, people ascend even low-lying mountains by a level path;
yet that army of Murāri ascended around the great mountains along the very paths themselves.
With clouds split by the tips of their tusks, the elephants looked upward and ascended massive mountain peaks;
their ears and inner temples were filled by rivers of rutting ichor flowing obliquely from their temples.
The path was blocked high up by a certain massive mountain, which possessed broad tusks and the splendor of a cluster of clouds, as it dripped drops of intoxicating water.
The trees were broken, scattering in all directions along with fluttering banners;
the elephants crushed the mountain ridges with their speed, and the earth became impassable due to the mountains of their own moving limbs.
Hari beheld more than a hundred elephants resting upon the mountains,
like massive boulders from the foothills cast down by a cataclysmic wind blowing against them.

The mountain women, who dwelt in groves of *āmalakī* trees, gazed upon him with eyes wide with the playfulness of blossoming beauty, their breasts— exceedingly full from the habit of climbing crags— resembling those very fruits.

Having opened his eyes for a moment with contempt, King Mṛgendra, wishing to sleep, did not even stir from the army; how much less would he have been pained by the god born of Rājaṃbha, or rather, by the God of Love? (MSV 12.52)

With banners that shook the trees growing upon them, with elephants that repeatedly hurled massive boulders, and with the force of their surging troops that crowded out the common folk, that army of theirs stood high above those mountains.
When the honeycomb was being scraped by the elephant as it rubbed its temple against the tree,
and when the people were agitated and bitten by swarms of bees— both small and even smaller— it fled.
When the Palāśinī tree, which was as dear to him as his own body, was led away by Gajāntaka— whose deeds bring an end to the pride of his enemies—
the monkeys in an instant moved from one tree to another, as if transferring their very selves into other bodies.
Now, at times exceedingly humble, at times resorting to haughtiness, and sometimes manifesting lightness or even depth,
the army of Hari then traversed those heavy mountains, which were devoid of equanimity.
Having surrounded even the trackless wastes on all sides with that army of his which could traverse every path,
he turned the rivers known as "opponents"— whose high banks had previously been impassable due to their waters— into those named "facing" (pratīpa).
Before the herds of elephants had even plunged in, the dust raised by the hooves of the horses was driven forward by the winds;
falling before the rivers, that very dust turned the water into mud.
Wandering repeatedly with pride, intoxicated by rut, their high haunches wounded by the friction [of the ground],
those elephants— resembling the rivers flowing to the sea— created mud that resembled the mossy garments pulled away by their trunks.
Having filled the hollows of the mountain slopes and leveled the ancient riverbeds with water, the elephants,
with the rut-fluid from their temples, set in motion other rivers whose floods were eroding the banks.
The rivers— devoid of lotuses, lacking the splendor of the faces of their brides, and bereft of swans that bring the beauty of parasols—
lay far behind the king as he proceeded like a mountain, his bracelets of lotuses slipping off.
With its herds of elephants— dark as collyrium from their recent bathing and towering without any gaps—
that army eclipsed the splendor of many cities whose palaces were washed with moonlight.
Along the road, the dwellings of the Lord shone with cloth tents that rivaled the exquisite beauty of palaces;
surely, at that time, the very Fortune of the City, distressed by separation from him, went out before him.

Roaring loudly, the bees— dwelling upon the trunks of trees that were melting with the ichor flowing from their cheeks as they rubbed them together— proclaimed for a long time to the forest-dwellers the towering stature of the elephants.
With hundreds of elephant herds possessing great length, which dwarfed the rows of high watchtowers,
and with tents that surpassed the lofty mansions, that army passed beyond many cities and proceeded on its way.
The dust, raised high by the rays of the sun and heated by its proximity,
fell before him into the waters of the Yamunā, stirred by the refreshing breezes from the *kahlāra* lotuses.
Though she is the daughter of the sun, she is cool; though she is the sister of Yama, she is the life-giver to people;
though she is black, she is most effective at destroying great sins with her waters, which purify even more than those prescribed by the creators.
From her, clouds as white as balls of snow rush forth like molten streams from the slopes of Mahānīla;
yet in an instant, they are colored by those [clouds] as if by Kālī, becoming like masses of crushed collyrium.
It is evident that if reason were more powerful than scripture, the Ganges would not have filled the ocean;
otherwise, how could its water have acquired the color of Śiva’s throat, which was scorched by the torrent of the Gaṅgā?
As he strove with speed to traverse the earth, that great river, dark as a tamāla tree and possessing the majesty of speech,
appeared for a moment before him like a boundary-line across the vast ocean of his army.
That river was crossed on all sides by boats moving swiftly with oars that were like feet,
while women, clinging to them as they spun in circles upon the waves, appeared to be swimming about.
First, the lords of elephants playfully surrounded his two shoulders for a moment;
then they immediately crossed the water made abundant by the flow of their own ichor streaming incessantly.
With nostrils quivering, neighing loudly with upturned faces, their tails spread wide,
ears pricked, necks held firm and raised, they crossed ahead with eyes fixed upon the bank.
Having crossed that river so exceedingly difficult to traverse— as if crossing a most weighty vow—
the bellowing of the horned cattle, as they ascended the great riverbanks with their horns, resounded loudly and was magnificent.
As it was being parted by the forces of the lords of the Yadus, the river shone with the dark luster of a buffalo’s horn;
marked by the camps of elephants as red as vermilion, it appeared like the long tress of the Earth.

Some crossed the navigable waters with their arms—arms that moved swiftly and without obstruction, held high, and did not abandon their natural strength; they were so massive that they seemed like other waves tossing up the surges.

That army, having suddenly crossed that river whose great banks were shattered by the clashing of the horns of wild bulls and whose crocodiles were dragged out by the heavy feet of intoxicated merchants, proceeded further along the path where the waters were churned by the vast circles of chariots belonging to the Lord of Fortune.
When it was heard that he had crossed the Yamunā, he could no longer be called "the son of asceticism";
from that time on, news of him circulated day and night throughout the king's city as he departed from his own home.
Then, as if intoxicated by the great joy born from the arrival of the Lord of the Yadus,
the king, accompanied by his younger brothers, suddenly went out from there to meet him in the city which was filled with even greater exultation.
Then, as the people’s hearing was deafened by the sounds of the drums of the Kuru host advancing with impetuosity,
the speakers conveyed the remainder of the intended meaning of their desired discourse by means of gestures with the hands.

And all around, within a mere step’s distance of the kings of the earth, fell the banners of those who possessed flags; their golden rims whirled rapidly, and the dust of the earth—stirred by the swift wind—served as their fluttering cloth.
The movements of the hooves of the horses upon the ground, which was torn up by their feet, were like the rapid beating of hand-drums;
and the peacocks, delighted by the deep trumpeting of the clouds that resembled the lowing of elephants, uttered their melodious cries as if they were dancing.

Even as the armies of the enemy of the Asuras and the son of Pāṇḍu were then moving toward a state of union out of affection, they were instantly struck by tuskers; for how can there be discernment among those whose intellects are deluded by intoxication?
As soon as the king beheld him from afar and desired to alight quickly from his chariot, the monkey descended first by himself; thus he distinguished his own humility by his eagerness.
With his body, upon which a broad string of pearls was being gathered on the ground before him, the Ancient Puruṣa—
though bowed down by the worlds— manifested his own majesty and prostrated himself before his father’s sister’s son.
Before he could touch the surface of the earth with his head, which was colored by the pollen-like rays of his crown,
the king, disregarding all formalities, impetuously seized him within the cage of his arms.
The chest of the enemy of Mura, broad as the surface of a door-panel, could not fit upon the body of the king;
nevertheless, he was embraced all around by the pair of the king’s long arms, which were spread wide.
Having surely abandoned her lotus, which had dwelt without interval upon her chest down to her navel,
the Fortune of the Enemy of Mura ascended to the face of the King of Kurus out of fear of his merciless squeezing.
Then the king smelled the head of Vinayavāmana— who, under the pretext of being Vāmana, had bound the enemy of the gods—
upon whose hair the fragrance of the celestial tree, won by his valor, seemed to linger like his own glory.
Although the birth of Vasudeva had been relaxed by her whose hair-pores were bristling with the sensation of joy,
the Kurupati’s creeper-like body did not lose its loveliness, which resembled a cluster of blossoming *kadamba* flowers.

Furthermore, being joyful and with eyes blossoming with delight, he— who was worthy of honoring people in an assembly and who had forcibly uprooted the host of asuras— honored the other kings born later than himself according to their rank.

Having approached, those lords of the earth— possessing equal splendor, as solid as stone, and endowed with arms longer than the wings of clouds— embraced the sovereigns of the earth, just as mountains beyond a thunderbolt embrace other mountains.
With their bellies held far away by the weight of each other’s breasts, which were as high and firm as the frontal globes of elephants,
and with their broad cheeks fully blooming, the women of the Kukuras and Kauravas embraced one another.
The two armies, crowded with chariots, horses, infantry, and female elephants, encountered one another;
yet the elephants alone kept their distance, for everything belonging to the great indeed transcends ordinary people.
Commanded by the king with the words, "Please ascend," the horse Hanumān, his trunk extended by the son of the Wind-god,
took hold of the sprout-like hand of Elāvilā and mounted the chariot, just as Indra mounts a cloud.
Then, as the enemy of Mura stood upon his chariot facing the three cities of his foe,
the Lord of Creatures, the embodiment of Dharma, moved by a spirit of affection, himself took up the reins.
Then, slowly, the son of the Wind-god [Hanumān] scattered his tail-fan, which resembled a mass of moonbeams shimmering through the lattice-work of his body,
like a great heap of foam from the lord of rivers.

Jiṣṇu received a sunshade that surpassed the splendor of a flock of swans upon the lake of the Yamunā; it was as white as a large moon and possessed a luster like that of a blooming *kalāya* flower, belonging to the Lord of the worlds.
Standing between the son of Pavana and the son of Indra, the radiant wielder of the discus shone intensely,
as if the moon were engaged in the yoga known as Durudharā, which occurs when it is situated between two planets.
Then, as he was the sovereign lord of the earth through its governance and policy— just as the rules of restraint and self-control follow a disciplined ascetic—
the two sons of the Aśvins attended upon him, like the Sun and Wind attending the Sun when it is surrounded by the glory of victory.
Then, as they approached their teacher-like enemy of the sons of Diti with joyful, humble, and blossoming devotion,
those who were themselves the chastisers of the undisciplined conducted themselves with great discipline.
Then, as those two armies met— indistinguishable from one another like the waters of the Yamunā and the Gaṅgā—
the heavens, with their celestial chariots echoing with sounds of joy, resounded as if with supreme delight.
The enemy of the sons of Danu beheld the city from the outside, where dwellings had been prepared all around for the kings who had come to witness the sacrifice,
and which seemed as if it were being besieged by the armies of those monarchs.
Filling the quarters of space with its echoing roar as it advanced toward the city gate,
that ocean-like army shone like the torrent of the Indus River surging toward the mouth of a cave in the Himalayas.
Having repeatedly assumed the birth of many bodies, that Puruṣa now entered the city, which possessed nine distinct inner gateways,
together with the five princes who were like his own sense-faculties.
In that place, men shone with bodies whose splendor surpassed even the form of the God of Love as it had never been gazed upon by the eyes of the Three-eyed One;
and women likewise shone with faces as beautiful as the moon, which far excelled the radiance of pulmonary consumption.
Then, summoned by the sounding of drums by the enemies of the gods' foes for the sake of a sight,
the city women went out into every street, hastening while disregarding all other duties.
Beholding the women who had completed their adornments and whose garments were slipping from hands that were busy holding them up,
the rows of palaces seemed to break into a loud laugh against the walls through the echoes of the drums.

In their haste, women rushed forward with necklaces, anklets, and girdles displaced, with their earrings resting upon their hair, their pairs of garments turned inside out, and their ear-ornaments serving as bracelets.
Under the influence of passion, a certain woman cast off her foot from the sprout-like hand of her maid;
she left a path marked by a single footprint of molten lac, like Pārvatī as she went to share half of Śiva’s body.
The women moved about, their noisy girdles jingling as they brushed against the peaks of the narrow balconies,
while their golden anklets tinkled as they stepped upon the lofty golden walkways of the mansions.
Resembling the gleaming golden lattice-window of his palace,
the face-lotus of Murajit shone with a desire to see [the sage], like the orb of the moon situated within the hollow of a cave on the mountain of sunrise.
As a certain woman ascended to her lofty residence with the hem of her garment fluttering in the wind,
the city, graced by her as it approached during the month of Mādhava, shone as if adorned with a banner.
In every house, the women scattered parched grain and flowers from their hands— which were like lotus buds—
over Priyarathāṅga, as if showering heaps of pearls released from the opened shells of oysters.
Radiant as the moon freed from frost, accompanied by lotuses, intoxicating the birds, and awakening the god of love,
that spring season— Mādhava— became for a long time a great festival for women, having propitiated the gods.
Out of fear of the Lord of the Earth, the Three-Eyed One clearly did not look at these women;
however, he gazed for a moment upon the playful damsels before him, who were empowered by Madana and thus free from fear.
The worlds were swallowed by the vast belly of the ocean-dweller at the end of the eon;
yet that very same being was drunk up, in turn, by the single glance of one woman among the city-folk, her eyes rolling with the intoxication of passion.
A certain woman, her breasts rising and falling as she repeatedly moved them, making a sound like that of a peacock’s tail-feathers or a conch shell,
quickly pressed her earlobe with the tip of her finger toward Kṛṣṇa.

With her hand, beautiful as the petal of a pale-red lotus and with its bud-like fingers repeatedly trembling, another woman called out to her rival— the enemy of Spring— with a nod of her head, her words being implicit in their meaning rather than explicitly uttered.

Another yawned, having concealed her beautiful face with one hand— the beauty of whose fingers was like that of a lotus stalk— and from the gaps between her quivering fingers, the radiant light of her teeth issued forth like sprouts.

With her hand like a young sprout, another woman held back her slipping garment; her slender line of body hair was made more prominent by the luster of the dark gems set in her bracelets, and her eyes were momentarily fixed upon Hari.
With her sweat-drops dispelled by the breeze from the fanning of the wings of bees whirled about by her own fragrance,
a certain woman appeared near Śauri with a body and a gaze that did not blink, like the presiding deity of the city itself.
"The tawny one approaches our eyes as if with thirst"—thus did the women of shapely hips lament;
yet even he who gazes at him constantly does not know him, for even he certainly does not reach satiety.
Disregarding his own departure for home, he remained for a moment as if fashioned by the hand of a painter;
the womenfolk, having reached a state of emptiness along with Acyuta, stood waiting like their own minds.
With languid bodies and intoxication, the beautiful-eyed women slowly returned toward their own homes,
their hands cupped like lotuses with large, outstretched eyes, filled to the brim by the flood of Madhava’s nectar they had quickly drunk.

Then Hari traversed the city streets, which had been purified by water scented with nine fragrances, where the thick smoke of incense created the illusion of dust, and where garments hung from numerous, lofty banners.

Having brought from Lake Bindusaras that beautiful *maṇidāru* wood, said to belong to Vārṣaparvaṇa, Maya constructed a palace that surpassed the splendor of the celestial abodes; he then immediately approached that assembly hall.
At nightfall, when falling upon the luster of the houses with slabs polished of silver that licked the sky,
the sun, free from its summer heat, seemed once again to enter the womb of the ocean of milk for a moment.
In the dwellings, the floors were fashioned of red gems, their interiors turned green by the rays of white jewels;
they carried forth water for the libations to the father of Jamadagni’s son, appearing like ponds with sparse moss.
And there, during the nights, the rows of houses constructed from masses of clear stone, which had attained oneness with the moonlight,
were passed by people for a long time as if in darkness, indicated only by the touch of their hands.
In that place, the rays of the moon— whose guilt for insulting the wives of the lotus-stalks was made manifest by the heaps of black stones in their dwellings at night—
were repeatedly struck down in secret by those who dwelt there, even though they were out of sight, out of respect for the moon.

In that place, upon the walls of their jewel-adorned palaces, the happy people experienced great joy with their beloved women reflected in the statues— even though those women turned away, burdened by modesty, as they faced them for the first time.
There, amidst clusters of emerald mansions, the people beheld deer with their faces repeatedly lowered in longing for grass,
their sprout-like rays clinging to the tips of their tongues as if they were holding morsels of fodder.
Near its banks, the trees shone with their own reflections appearing in the mirror of the water filling their vast basins,
as if they were displaying a mass of roots together with a heap of leaves.

In his courtyard, the ground of the jeweled floor— its sprouts being the gems from the hair on the head of the lord of serpents— began to bud anew as it was repeatedly moistened by the spray from the thundering clouds that rose high above him.
And there, the lotus pond with its hidden waters— upon which Suyodhana had fallen, thinking it to be dry land—
became the cause for the destruction of all the kings who were agitated by the laughter of the Wind-god’s son.
In that place, where the ground was made of sapphire and shimmered all around with the soft luster of the swords brandished by those wishing to provoke laughter,
people repeatedly mistook the sky for water and drew it far away from them.
Then, from the chariot whose body shone with a circle of stainless rays, Hari and the Pāṇḍava descended toward the assembly hall—
delights to the eyes, like the moon and Venus descending from the sky onto the mountain of sunrise.

Then, as the king respectfully directed him from here to there, saying "Go this way, go that way," he slowly entered the assembly hall, where the entrance was made indistinguishable by the mass of rays from white gems upon its walls of invisible jewels.
Then, in that assembly, he beheld the king’s palace, constructed with bricks of fresh gold, which,
by the mass of its sky-touching jewel-lustre, put to shame even the dwellings of the gods on Mount Udaya.

Then the King and Acyuta sat down upon their seats of great splendor; they bore an impossible radiance, like that of the Lord of Day and the Full Moon shining simultaneously upon the peak of the mountain of sunrise.

The water of the ocean brought great joy to the royal family through the delight of the descendant of Yadu, who dispelled all fatigue like a breeze from the Malaya mountains with its heat; it was as if the moon had brought delight to the ocean.

The soft new songs, though fresh, possessed the quality of being never-before-heard, moving with faultless rhythm and melody; and the company of graceful dancing girls performed a brilliant dance, manifesting clear *sāttvika* emotions through their physical gestures.
When Hari had arrived there with his entire retinue, the king proclaimed a festival throughout the city that was to last until the end of time;
indeed, because of his great joy and impetuosity, the monarch surely forgot his own purpose.
Hari, who knew all names, questioned Ākumāra regarding the welfare of his own people;
for even after attaining great fortune, a noble person is never astonished and never forgets anything. (MSpv 13.68)
Attaining that which is difficult to obtain in the world of mortals— an arising of aesthetic delight characterized by ever-newness and abundance—
the Lord of Fortune and this Lord of the Earth both tasted the manifold nectar of their mutual conversation.

Speaking as if pouring forth his speech with a gaze that blossomed with affection, the king, the best among those skilled in eloquence, spoke to him while fixing his mind upon the sacrificial rite. (MSpv 14.1)
When another speaks what is pleasing, they feel no shame; rather, it is the speaker who experiences excessive embarrassment.
Yet, by speaking what is pleasing to you, even this venerable person of yours is filled with modesty.
Others find satisfaction in false praises, and such are easily obtained by embodied beings;
yet for you, there is no untrue word of praise, and you do not take pleasure even in that which is worthy of praise.
O All-Seeing One, even though this person speaks much that is pleasing to you, he does not fall into falsehood;
for all perfections of virtue exist in you, who are untainted by any fault.
That abundance of power and excellence is yours in even greater measure for the sake of the future,
since today this land of Bhārata, bearing its heavy burden, remains under my control.
O Lord, by granting me your favor through your permission, you have become the root for one who desires to attain the seven-fold sacrifice;
and as you have become that root, I have attained the state of being a tree composed of Dharma.
Having gathered the necessary provisions and desiring to perform a stainless sacrifice,
I have been waiting for you, O Wind, just as a farmer who wishes to ripen his grain waits for the breeze.
Now that this sinless sacrifice has been performed by me in your presence, free from all obstacles,
who is able to obstruct it— just as one might seek to thwart the splendor of the day when the moonless sun has risen?

"Whatever wealth I acquired in accordance with dharma, protected, and increased—that, as one who goes to the sacred fords, I shall offer according to the ritual; please partake of it and let me sacrifice it into the fire."
"O dear one, first you yourself must offer the oblation, or else after you have bathed in the purificatory rite (avabhṛtha);
then, once you have become a drinker of Soma, I shall sacrifice with the most excellent and desired ritual. (MSpv 14.10)
"What should be done with this abundance of wealth won through your grace?
Command me, O Ruler of the three worlds; I am your obedient servant, along with my younger brother."
To him who was speaking thus, Viṣṭaraśravas, making all the kings hear,
then spoke, his body variegated by the circles of light from his teeth.
This great majesty of yours has now subdued all kings solely through the excellence of your own conduct;
does that quality belong to another [if it were used], even if one follows a wholesome regimen and yet attains freedom from disease?
While that noble queen remains, who else could perform a sacrifice characterized by royalty?
Or, when she has been raised up, who else on earth would possess the fitness to do so, were it not for Śrī-Varāha?
Even within the Teaching, you may employ me as you wish in matters requiring heavy responsibility;
do not think of me as being anything other than one whose sole purpose is your own interest, O Dhanañjaya.
Whosoever here, at your sacrifice, shall perform his duty like a mere laborer rather than a lord,
even Sudarśana, the kinsman of the worlds, shall reduce his body to a headless trunk.

When these words had been spoken, the King, filled with joy, said to Śauri, "Since you are established in the highest good, my every prosperity shall be secure," and he rose to proceed with the sacrifice.
Bearing a digit of the moon upon his face, having diminished the physical form of Kāma by his very appearance,
and bathed in pure waters, he became the eighth manifestation of the eight-formed Lord Śiva.
For him, who bore a resemblance to the Sāṃkhya Puruṣa by not performing actions himself,
agency arose through the perception [of those actions] in the instrument that undergoes the activity, just as it does in the officiating priest.
Those who know the characteristics of speech uttered the wordless invocation loudly with the *anuvākyā*,
while those performing the act of sacrifice offered the oblation after designating the deity by means of the *yājyā*.
The Sāma-vids sang the Sāman with the tone fashioned by the seventh musical interval, free from attachment;
and there the wise ones, their speech truthful and pleasant, recited the holy Ṛg and Yajus verses.
Gazed upon by the sacrificer’s wife, who wore a girdle made of darbha grass,
they offered the oblations into the fire that had been consecrated by the rites of leading forward and other preparations.
In that scripture, it is not possible to state [the ritual] directly through all the case-endings and individual forms;
therefore, the practitioner skilled in the adaptation of mantras applies them by modifying the accusative case.
Regarding two compounds that possess identical forms but yield vastly different results in terms of their grammatical function,
those learned in the science of grammar sought to determine the analysis (*vigraha*) of each by means of the accent.
The Fire-god, as if laughing with his radiant halo— the hundredfold lolling tongues of flame—
repeatedly licked up the abundant, stainless clarified butter consecrated with the *vaṣaṭ* call.
There, as he consumed the oblation purified by mantras during the sacrifice, it was not only his physical form that shone;
for the eater of the oblation also assumed a name of brilliant splendor, one that possessed an exceedingly clear excellence of syllables.
That the fire, possessing its accustomed hot touch, did not burn the sacrificial oblation was not surprising;
yet it consumed the flood of the sins of embodied beings even by its mere scent arising from the offered oblations.
Rising suddenly, turning the quarters of the sky grey and surpassing the clouds in density,
the banner of the Fire-god ascended to heaven, as if proclaiming the welcome news to the denizens of the celestial realm.
The gods vomited forth the nectar—the essence of the flow of medicinal herbs from all the great oceans they had conquered;
they were barely able to endure waiting while it was being offered into the fire.
There, among the celestial women whose husbands were away on journeys,
their braided hair remained woven upon their heads instead of the garlands of blossoming divine trees that they customarily wore.
Because they swiftly consumed the oblation here, they attained long-lasting immortality;
and the gods, their vital energy increased by that superior offering, conquered the arrogant Dānavas.
No ritual action whatsoever suffered any deficiency; every means of accomplishment was perfectly fulfilled therein.
The wisdom of the officiating priests and the prosperity of the king surpassed one another.
Having recognized the assembly of twice-born men, who were worthy of offerings and purifiers of the row,
the skillful king distributed in that hall the sacrificial fees for the Rājasūya, one by one.

together with your followers, rise high above even the greatest of mountains.
May the streets in your cities be difficult to approach on all sides due to throngs of elephants resembling dense clouds, and may they be filled with wild deer and other creatures.

May your enemy— whose own prowess is completely eclipsed, whose rise is increased by certain downfall, who is devoid of high-mindedness and courage, and who is devoid of policy— be for you a constant disease.

O bull among the Yadus, as you entered into combat with the King of Cedi, his wine— along with its divine spirit— was poured upon you out of affection for your kinsman, like fresh nectar falling upon one whose eyes are as beautiful as blooming blue lotuses.
Anaka-dundubhi having set out with his army, you, together with Sāraṇa and mace in hand,
should swiftly approach him in battle to confront him.
Having now encountered Śiśupāla, who has been slaying his enemies in battles,
may you dwell for a long time together with all the Sātvatas, surrounded by trusting and playful women.

The lord of the earth, filled with joy and accompanied by his attendants, repeatedly gazed upon you— who had conquered anger, who were honored by great beings, who had repeatedly defeated and subdued your enemies, and who stood before him— as he looked upon the enemy of those great mountain-like kings.
Having thus addressed the enemy's spy who stood there silently, Sātyaki,
his single eyebrow twitched by the wielder of the discus (Kṛṣṇa), then spoke these words as if urged on.
O skillful one, you have spoken words that are sweet on the outside but unpleasant within;
yet, because they contain the complete truth, they are perceived as pleasant within while being unpleasant on the outside.
On one side your speech is exceedingly tender, while on the other it is as coarse as the stalk of a fresh lotus; thus it clearly possesses the dual nature of a leaf of the *śāka* plant.
One should be as wary of such a person— who speaks with apparent gentleness while secretly indicating harsh intentions—
as one would be of an ill-omened bird perched on the path.
If the lord of the earth has worshipped Hari, what jealousy can there be in you, a king, over this? Who would feel resentment toward a fragrant flower placed upon the head? (MSpv 16.20)
Ah, how exceedingly delicate is the heart of the young, for they suddenly vomit forth whatever unpleasantness has entered it; indeed, the wise digest such things.
The virtuous person is by nature constantly intent on benefiting all people;
yet, alas, their very eminence causes incessant and deep-seated heartache to the wicked.
The superior person feels distress only when they themselves are afflicted; another, who is well-restrained, feels distress even when others are afflicted;
but the base person, whose evil aspirations are laid bare and shattered, feels pain at the prosperity of others.

How could a wise person resort to wickedness— which lacks the excellence of asceticism, is devoid of fruit, and is abandoned by the virtuous— just as one would not approach an unchaste woman who is likewise devoid of the wealth of penance, barren of offspring, and shunned by noble-minded men?
Keśava gave no reply to the King of Cedi as he uttered his curse;
for a lion does not echo the roar of a cloud with the howls of a jackal.

For those of great intelligence who have immediately conquered the torrent of anger, even a person conquered by anger is insignificant; what cause for conflict can there be with the wise for one of evil mind who has already been conquered by that which has itself been conquered? (MSpv 16.26)

The greatness of the truly exalted does not indeed depart because of the arrogant words of the wicked; for does the high value of a gem diminish when it is covered by the dust of the soil? (MSV 16.27)
There is no embodied being who possesses any internal quality that could satisfy them;
yet, it is said that the petty man desires to please his own kin with talk of others' faults.
Those whose vision is naturally blind to their own misconduct yet possess the divine eye to perceive the faults of others;
those who speak highly of their own virtues while observing the vows of sages, yet are unskilled in acknowledging the excellence of others. (MSV 16.29)

Even when great skill is manifest, noble-minded people are exceedingly adept at concealing for a long time what might be criticized by others, yet they are equally skilled at revealing their own virtues.

What great-minded person would proclaim his own virtues, which are already celebrated by the whole world? No one else would speak of his own virtues unless he were very base; therefore, he speaks of them himself. (MSV 16.31)
Others, free from boastfulness, release their anger like venomous serpents;
they possess an internal essence, while others are merely hollow sounds like kettledrums.
If that King of Cedi desires to see the end of hell, let him come quickly by whatever means prescribed; I shall not fail to provide him with a fitting response.
If this king, having girded himself for battle, desires to make peace with him, it is impossible that Hari should bow down out of fear at the onset of an attack; indeed, such a thing cannot happen.
The evil-minded person perishes through his own fault by rashly overstepping what is great;
surely the blazing flame does not of its own will make the moths its fuel.
That which the lord of the earth had not previously fulfilled himself with his own mouth for a hundred years,
he has now fully accomplished through the mouth of a messenger on behalf of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Whatever unpleasant thing you shall speak from this unbarred gateway,
it will cause our anger— long preserved by waiting for the right moment— to burst forth at last.

Having heard those powerful words of Śini’s grandson, the descendant of Anarta, the messenger—casting aside his fear once more—spoke these words to his enemies: *niśamya tadūrjitaṃ śinervacanaṃ napturanāpturenasām / punarujjhitasādhvaso dviṣāmabhidhatte sma vaco vacoharaḥ //* MS Pṛ 16.38 Hearing that formidable speech of Śini’s grandson, the great-grandson of Anarta and one free from sin, the messenger, having again cast off his trepidation, addressed these words to the foes.
The ordinary person, whose intellect is perverse, does not discern his own welfare even by himself;
that he does not understand this even when it is proclaimed by others is a great marvel.
The wise either believe in the impending calamity through their own insight or from another;
however, the person of small intellect does not measure what is presented by another nor even from themselves, except through direct experience.
O Kṛṣṇa, it was indeed for your own benefit that I spoke those words;
for the virtuous are intent on giving instruction even to others who are headed toward their own destruction. (MSpv 16.41)
Both conciliation and its opposite have been uttered by me to you simultaneously;
having distinguished them separately with your own intelligence, you shall surely perform that which accords with your own virtue.
Alternatively, well-spoken words become useless among those whose minds are possessed by dogmatic attachment,
just as the web of rays from the cool-rayed moon becomes useless upon lotus-pools that are scorched by the sun.
Disregarding merits and faults, people follow their own inclinations with certainty;
indeed, the elder brother of Bhīma abandoned the lord of the earth and worshipped you instead.

If the King of Cedi, the elder of the Kurus, was not honored by you out of devotion, was the gem born from the forehead of an elephant blameworthy simply because it was rejected by the lion, who loves meat? (MSpv 16.45)
Indeed, that which is white above is made even whiter by those very white things, while that which is below is made darker by those other than white;
Śaṅkara bore the celestial river upon his head, while the conqueror of Madhu bore it at his feet.
How could there even be fitness for you, whose mind has been made arrogant by fools, with the sons of Pṛthā?
For a guñjā berry, though attended by monkeys, does not attain heat. (MSV 16.47)
The king surpasses you with a single quality—forgiveness—which endures even a hundred offenses;
for even though you abducted the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, he remained forgiving toward you, since he was indeed capable of retaliation.

"O Janārdana, having abducted the bride bestowed by your elders from the presence of your own kinsman, the king, you are clearly the progenitor of the Mind-born (Kāma), who has utterly destroyed both dharma and artha."

Just as the sun, casting away darkness whose form cannot be defined and which possesses the hue of a cuckoo’s plumage, now drives it away, so does the king, O all-pervading one, dispel [the darkness] from you.
To offer a means of pacification to you regarding this agitated king is futile for me;
what can a mere channel do for the world when the ocean surges at the time of universal dissolution?
Sent by the king to summon the descendant of Madhu to the great battle, I have come;
for those of great splendor do not harm their enemies through deceit, unlike common thieves.
Therefore, this king approaches like an irresistible flood of water;
become a reed without delay, O Madhava, and do not break like a tree.
Do not place your trust in his name, "He protects only children";
for that patient refuge-seeker protects even the youths—the enemies who have come to him for shelter.
How could others, intent on their own interests, venture to do something unpleasant to the Great One without hesitation?
For even when angry, that noble-minded one accepts conciliation with a mere bow of the head.
If you desire to hear what is beneficial though unpleasant, then make peace before you perish;
but if you find satisfaction in false and pleasing words, then live on, O Lord of the Earth, and may you be victorious!
"Though you are the conqueror of adversaries, there is no doubt that you will be defeated in battle by the King of Cedi;
for does not darkness repeatedly swallow the sun, the lord of day, who dispels the gloom, even though he is named Rāhu?"
Before long, that king— whose power overcomes the god of love, who shines while being honored by the hosts of Vṛṣṇis,
and who has subdued the arrogant Antaka (Death)— will emulate the playful majesty of Hara.
Having slain a fierce elephant in rut and thereby acquired great fame through his own prowess, this king does not fear even Hari in battle; what need is there to mention the Vṛṣṇis?
It is no wonder that his enemies do not look upon his face in battle out of fear;
for even he never looks at the backs of his fleeing foes.
Having encountered autumn, their weapons shattered and their lightning flashes now but faintly shimmering,
the clouds— though they carry water— are equal to his enemies only if they do not bear arrows.
His pair of feet, first soiled by the dust of battle and repeatedly washed by the tears of his enemies' wives,
is then anointed with the pigments of the radiance from the crowns of kings.
And at the mere moment his bow is drawn for battle— extremely harsh [in its action]—
the host of his enemies, fearing defeat, quickly bows down along with that very bow.
Friends perceive this cool-rayed moon as having hot rays, while enemies perceive it otherwise;
just as those whose vision is distorted by their own actions see a garland as a serpent, and others see it as such.
Maintaining bodies that were difficult to find, indestructible, and superhuman through their exclusive devotion,
his enemies— though equal to the gods— are currently not established upon this earth.
For that king whose every deed was most wonderful, there was nothing whatsoever that was contrary [to his will];
he brought to destruction the entire lineage of those who were hostile toward him, even as they were intent on their own ruin.
With the abundance of his upper body swaying and his path blocked by a formation of sea-monsters,
he repeatedly crossed vast oceans of battle by the power of his own arms.
He who, puffed up with pride, does not wish to bow his head before the feet of a king,
shall, once his pride has vanished, place that very foot upon his own head.
Armed solely with his two arms as weapons, he abandoned his fourfold army and repeatedly engaged in battle against the four-tusked elephant of Śakra.
Between you two, whose beautiful wheels are unshaken and who are embraced by Śrī out of affection, this alone is the difference:
that you are Upendra, while he is indeed Atīndra (the one beyond Indra).
Though he possesses the power of the elements and enjoys inexhaustible pleasures, having conquered many cities of his enemies,
this unborn lord of the earth, whose splendor is like that of the full moon, inspires longing for the crescent moon.
Relying on his great loftiness, he who possesses an unbreakable rise swiftly leads others to sudden downfall;
yet he causes another, whose arm-branches quiver upon the surface of the earth, to attain extreme elevation.
Having discovered a vulnerability within and causing a breach of the circle elsewhere, he instantly digs up the great roots of someone whose cohesion has been shattered. (MSV 16.73)
Drawing some by force from among his followers who carry thick leaves, he makes them his own;
yet another, though firmly established and even hostile, he utterly casts away.
Thus, like a flood of water from rivers born of the rainy season that has broken through the trees on its banks,
he whose progress is nowhere obstructed sports with hosts of kings.
Adorned with rows of heavy ornaments and completely obstructing the surrounding space,
these girdles, having ascended to the regions of their hips, do not leave them for a long time.
Their arms, adorned with beautiful ornaments of fresh pearls, bear bracelets;
and they certainly maintain an inseparable connection with their broad cheek-mountain slopes by means of their variegated [ornaments].
Thus, those very same women who formerly enjoyed all manner of prosperity in their palaces have now clearly met with total calamity upon the summits of the mountains.
Though he burns like a forest fire the great Kukura, Andhaka, and Drumas to an extreme degree, it is most extraordinary that this lord of the earth will leave the earth not blackened [by his smoke].
Though composed of few syllables, his command has pervaded every object and attained firm establishment;
indeed, like a most weighty legal decree, it is never obstructed by anything whatsoever. (MSV 16.80)
That very Punarbhū, whom the ancient Puruṣa, assuming the form of a boar at the beginning of time, married for a moment,
is now being properly wedded once again by him who has destroyed his enemies, remaining entirely unharmed.

Although both the waves of the ocean and his own great virtues are equally vast and, for the most part, never fail in their loftiness, the waves of the sea perish upon reaching the shore, whereas his great waves of virtue do not.
The light of the sun, obstructed by the Lokāloka mountain, is unable to spread even as it strives;
yet the brilliance of him who stands at the forefront of the world quickly and boldly ascends high over the mountains.
The bodies of their enemies were adorned with fresh sandalwood paste, their lips stained with lac, their eyes fell into clear collyrium, and their hips shone with girdles;
thus, the young women of those foes possessed eternal ornaments both in times of prosperity and in times of calamity.

Having immediately struck down you, whose splendor was so great, in battle, he will— his heart filled with compassion for the throngs of your weeping women— make the name Śiśupāla (the "Crying Child") true to its meaning.

When these words had been spoken by that eloquent one— words as formidable as the wind agitated at the end of an eon— the assembly immediately became as turbulent as the ocean, rising up like the great dissolution of the world.
With passion, with sweat flowing from their thick bodies like perspiration, with the broad surfaces of their thighs resounding from the blows of their hands,
and with lips repeatedly bitten by their teeth, the kings approached him in anger as if they were approaching a most beloved woman.
As Gada struck his own shoulder with the palm of his hand, shattering his armlet in an instant,
it appeared as if the fire of his wrath were clearly bursting forth, accompanied by sparks from the brilliantly flashing, shattered pieces of red stone.
When Bala laughed loudly out of contempt, the circle of rays from his gleaming teeth momentarily restored his own natural luster to his body, even though it had been turned crimson by his wrath.

As Ulmuka rushed forward with his wide circle of flying necklaces whirling rapidly, he struck his shoulders against the hard surface of a massive stone slab; consequently, the entire assembly seemed as if it were spinning in a circle.

As Yudhājit grew enraged, the lotus of his face broke into a sweat once more, as he vigorously fanned it with the air from the hem of his garment, which was heated by the impact of the wind of his sighing breath.
The people perceived Niṣadha, who had arisen for the purpose of performing the Prajāpati sacrifice, as a fierce and haughty fever;
