they saw him, filled with extreme wrath, suddenly prepared to slay his enemies, like an incurable disease.

The two hands of Sudhanvan, which were mutually enraged and crushed one another until they were smeared with the dust of golden rings from their wounds, were instantly washed by his own incessantly flowing streams of blood.
Āḷavaka extended his forefinger, which was long, blazing with the flame of fire, and possessed a halo created by the radiance of his glowing nails;
its form was like a flickering firebrand that does not waver, as if he intended to burn the world.
Manmatha became so difficult to behold that even Hara, it seems,
could no longer bear to look upon him with his third eye— him who had previously displayed such audacity in burning [Kāma] before his very eyes.
Reflecting on the battle that had presented itself,
Pṛthu, out of passion, stroked with his fingertips his chest where the hair stood erect and which was stripped of sandalwood paste by the firm and hard breasts of his beloved.
Seeing that even the preceptor, the son of Gāndinī, had transgressed the bounds of decorum due to his enemy’s harsh words,
the people then perceived the lords of mountains to be overturned by the winds at the end of an eon.
Rolling his eyes, which were clouded with intoxication, and uttering a terrifying roar as he struck the earth with his trunk,
Prasenajit— his body turned deep red with rage— became like an elephant stained crimson by red chalk.
Covered with drops of water as dense as saffron and as red as ripe pomegranates— which he sought out—
the elephant shone for a long time as if drenched in droplets of blood issuing from his body split open by rage.

With the sunbeams— whose paths were opened by the fissures in the earth burst open by the frantic stamping of his feet— he brought the netherworld (Rasātala), where serpents were tormented by the unaccustomed heat, into the light.
The rays of the golden crown, flashing like lightning, flicker at every moment upon his head as he seeks refuge;
they seem to make the lords of the earth lose their luster, as if announcing, "Now these kings shall enter battle without fear."
With his wide, vine-like arms outstretched, Vidūratha, desiring to speak, opened his cavernous mouth,
which was terrifying with its quivering lower lip, like a tree spreading its great branches and revealing a hollow with a moving serpent within.
Even so, in that tumultuous assembly, the mind of the Destroyer of Mura did not undergo any change due to the words of others;
for the water of the ocean does not undergo transformation by the waters of rivers swollen with the rain from heavy clouds.
"Since others, while censuring us, praise themselves, this is the way of the wicked"— thinking thus,
Uddhava, remaining unperturbed, brought about no change in his countenance, which was as lovely as the autumnal moon, save for a smile.
When the spies had been driven away by the enraged Yādavas and had slowly departed from that place of the enemies,
the army of the Foe of Mura then, in an instant, equipped itself for victory with its drums sounding terrifyingly.

In battle, the Vṛṣṇi kings— whose teeth of undiminished valor bit their lips, and whose massive bodies, burdened by broad hips, repeatedly stumbled over the weapons of their enemies— showed their persons to him, saying, "This is the right course."

For other kings, difficult to bear even for a moment, their armor quickly swelled with pride upon hearing of that battle; yet for those sovereigns who possessed true majesty, neither the joys within their bodies nor the armor on their exterior could expand.
The kings themselves, who were already urging on their herds of elephants, their armored chariots, their horses yoked for victory, and their swift steeds,
repeatedly exhorted those officials in charge of them to act with even greater haste.
Then, with their girth-bands firmly tightened for battle against the enemies, the herd of elephants— accompanied by the humming songs of swarms of bees—
themselves offered an inexhaustible flow of ichor from the hollows of their trunks along with water.
With beautiful girdles, lovely with their exceedingly white teeth, and possessing the splendor of shimmering, fine lower garments, the sword-blades—
bearing bristling hair like horripilation— hung down from the necks of those seeking battle like beloved women.

Murajit was served by his weapons, which were captivating in their natural beauty yet terrifying in appearance during battles; they were like his own limbs, always present and never departing from him.
Then, having traveled unimpeded many times among both the royal camps and even within the enemy armies,
he mounted his chariot, whose rims were repeatedly drenched with the blood of hundreds of gods' enemies wounded in battle.
And having approached, with the wind from his own wings causing the distant quarters of the sky to turn tawny with his radiance,
the Lord of Birds at that moment took his station upon the top of the banner-pole, which was shaken though it was exceedingly firm.
Then, delighting the vocal peacocks with the beauty of its sound— which surpassed the resonance of the deep-toned mṛdaṅga drum and which robbed the enemy swans of their joy—
that chariot set forth like a fresh rain-cloud.
Then, observing the massing army which completely filled the quarters of the sky,
the people lost all curiosity regarding the ordinary great flood, as it was like the waters of the ocean surging forth without restraint.
Lordly elephants with great tusks swelled with strength, victorious horses neighed loudly,
and the mountain caves, unable to contain their roar, seemed at that time to have their very foundations shattered by the sound.
As the drum of the Enemy of Madhu resounded incessantly for victory with light echoes from its wooden frame,
the mountains— through their cave-mouths where lions were rushing out— seemed to laugh with supreme joy.
As the roar of the celestial host entered the caves of the mountain of the gods, deafening the path of their hearing,
the skillful amorous cooings of clever women during the intervals of their lovemaking became utterly useless.
Desiring to seize those slain in battle by their enemies while they were fighting alongside [the gods], and having heard the sounds of the war-trumpets,
the celestial courtesans prepared their adornments, which had long been abandoned but were now appropriate for their first reunion.
Urged on by mahouts who were well-trained in their duties and skilled in the use of the goad,
the elephants— struck once with the tubes held in the palms of their hands— advanced repeatedly while their bells rang out.
With their fly-whisks scattered here and there, moving as they strode with vigorous steps, they seemed to scatter the dust of the earth;
indeed, the eyes of the people could not cease gazing upon the horse bearing its fresh trappings.
She danced with her trunk raised, its bud-like fingers moving, while clearly beating a rhythm against her ears;
she was sung to in sweet tones by swarms of bees clinging to her temples, which were wet with the fluid of rut.
The earth, its dust laid to rest, was sprinkled with the waters of rut by her who held a fresh, full pitcher;
and musical instruments, heavy with the sound of rising clouds and pleasing to the ear, were sounded by her faces.
There were banners reaching to the sky, their cloths fluttering in the wind, standing indifferent here and there;
for before the enemy of the foes of Śārṅgin, an auspicious array of elephants had been personally formed.
This dwelling place did not reach emptiness even when the army, though possessing great strength, moved upon it;
for even when the ocean rushes toward the earth at the end of an eon, it does not indeed become empty.

Then the people, wishing to go toward the city of Madhubhid (Mathurā) with the Sun-god, perceived the direction before them— grey with the horns of aged buffaloes, garlanded by the dust of the advancing enemy forces— to be as if smoky.
The sound of his own mṛdaṅga drums was not heard by the wise as clearly as the roar of the enemy host, which,
rising up for battle before him, captivated the minds of all with its tumultuous din.
Just as the sound of the drum drew closer to the lake before the foremost of the monkeys,
so too did the army of the enemies become thrilled in body and agitated with joy in their hearts, like women.
Then, as the sky suddenly expanded, the line of enemy banners, dusted with pollen whirled up by the wind,
appeared from afar like the dark form of the Kali age born at the dissolution of the world.

In an instant, that army of asuras— though terrifying and exceedingly difficult to behold due to the swords flashing with light from the opposing rays of their sharp weapons— nevertheless attained a state of great beauty in the eyes of the mountain-dwellers.
As the clouds rushed swiftly through the sky, that mass of water, like a reversal of the heat of the sun,
spread across the surface of the earth in an instant, its flow uniform over both level and uneven ground.
As he gazed for a moment before him at that vast [form] containing the three worlds within its slender belly,
the great power of his enemies was utterly swallowed up within the wide and long eye of the Slayer of Madhu.
With bodies bristling with horripilation and perspiring profusely, their hearts filled with intense emotion and daring having taken root within them,
the hosts of wives in the enemy kings' armies suddenly became as agitated at the prospect of battle as women are at the onset of sexual passion.
With their banners spread wide by the favorable winds,
the enemies, having forcibly summoned them on, rushed toward the Yadus with weapons raised in fury, attaining the utmost speed.
The soldiers of Hari also advanced against the enemy forces with their chariots;
for high-minded men, seeing an enemy intent on conflict, are indeed not inclined to delay.

On the field of battle, the kings, their bodies covered with fitted breastplates from which rays of light issued like needles from shimmering gems, shone without interval as if strewn with heaps of autumnal flowers.
Then the dust of the earth, white as the mass of feathers on the necks of aged pigeons,
rose up high, driven upward by the folds of the ground as his moving feet shook it, scattering the rows of thick clouds.
In some places, the dust— its exit blocked from above by horses that were violently entangled with one another,
and struck at every step by their shifting hooves— wandered for a long time only along the ground.

For the more powerful one, who possesses many mouths and is full of passion, there arose a fierce *rajas* that obscured the *sattva*; but for the lotus-born Brahmā, who desires to create the world and wishes to remove its destruction, [there arose *sattva*].
"Long ago in battle, the blood produced by arrow wounds was forcibly turned into mud for us"—
certainly thinking thus, the flames of the fire-god’s banner, seized with fear, leapt high into the sky.
In some places variegated by dense clusters of shimmering clouds, in others tawny with heaps of golden dust,
and in others white as fragments of the autumnal moon, the dust raised from the ground trampled by hooves rose upward.
In the vast dust raised by the armies of elephants from the ends of the earth, which clung to their faces,
the dark bands of water from the clouds— already soiled by the rows of cuckoos— could no longer be distinguished as they were spread abroad.
"Let these youths not vainly perish in battle with hair as tender as a swarm of bees;
they are surely like old men whose hair has turned white through the pride of their strength"—thus did the dust make people appear as if aged.
Even one who possesses great splendor is undoubtedly brought into obscurity by many adversaries when they are well-united;
for the minute particles of the earth’s constituent parts obscured even the body of the sun, the treasury of light.
Enveloped by the thick dust rising from the earth wounded by the wheels of chariots moving with swift speed,
the world appeared as if submerged in the waters of the ocean at the moment of the destruction of the eon, when all restraints have ceased.

The quarters of the sky, like women whose faces were the shimmering rays of the sun, now in their menses with the beauty of their garments— their clouds— faded away, became for a moment unfit to be gazed upon, and thus became objects to be avoided by living beings.
Gathering in the sky out of curiosity to behold the prowess of the kings at the front of the battle,
the throngs of gods fled, for the dust that spread through the air caused pain to their lotus-like eyes, which did not blink.
As the wind, marked by its banner, blew with its brilliance momentarily extinguished and clung to every step while drinking up the waters,
the clouds— now heavy with accumulated mud and having ceased their rain— gradually moved away.
With their bodies washed by contact with the celestial river as they moved through the sky,
the elephants of the quarters experienced the pleasure of being bathed in the dust of the earth rising from the impact of the hooves of the moving army horses.
As the entire subterranean realm was pressed down by the earth sinking under the weight of the advancing herds of elephants,
and the vault of heaven was filled with the densest dust, the three worlds clearly seemed to attain a state of oneness.
The great caves of the mountains, filled with the dust raised by the armies that leveled their crevices,
became a necessary resource for the denizens of the sky who were seeking brides distressed by shame over their secret trysts.
Even when thick dust stood in the path of their vision like a veil covering their faces,
the elephants, with the scent of rutting ichor and the fragrance of honeyed mangoes carried by the wind, continued to charge impetuously toward other elephants.
The people beheld the elephants below, whose masses of dust were settled by the water trickling down in seven streams,
appearing like great cloth pavilions with thick circles of dust suspended above them.
Neither deficient nor protruding, exceedingly broad and bearing the splendor of mountains, they displayed a likeness to streaks of lightning through their golden chains;

raining down dust that served as a cosmetic for the elephant-like clouds, these clouds—whose dark bodies resembled the serpent Kāliya—brought peace at the proper time with their weapons of rainbow-streaked peaks.
Those two oceans of armies, heedless of retreat and roaring with deep sounds, met together with speed,
as if the Vindhya and Sahya mountains, desiring to nestle together in one place before their wings were clipped.
Foot soldier approached foot soldier, horseman went toward horseman, elephant toward elephant, and chariot-rider toward chariot-rider;
thus, through passion, the army of one side joined limb with limb of the opposing force, as if out of love for their beloved.
The continuous roar of the chariots, the trumpeting of the elephants, and the neighing of the horses,
pervading the sky, became an indistinct sound like that of the drums of the Lord.
As they advanced toward the enemy out of a fit of rage, with their thick arms raised high like banners,
the long sword-blades of the foot soldiers shone like transverse victory-pennants.
The golden breastplates of the cavalrymen, fastened with leather straps as they galloped with the *dhaurita* gait and leaping high,
shone like the personified forms of pride itself pervading their entire bodies.
With their thick-skinned flanks pressed against the couch, attaining a fourth degree of bodily splendor,
those elephants moved violently like boulders from mountain slopes driven by the wind at the end of an eon.

As he playfully raised his forequarters out of passion for the spirited horse that had stood up, the axle-pins of the chariots, sharing in its speed, broke, and the crowd greeted the victor with cries of "Alas! and "Ha! (hāhākāra).
The banners fluttering high upon the standards shone like brooms being raised to sweep away the abundant dust that obstructs the passage to the next world for those who are dying.
As the sun rose, bows were drawn by archers with harsh sounds, and elephants' heads were vigorously struck by elephant-riders with large, thick clubs that formed high circles.

The sound of the bells, the resonance of the kettledrums, and the tinkling of the neck-ornaments seemed to answer the words of the elephant-drivers intended to rouse the elephants' spirits by saying, "So be it! (Āma). (MSV 18.10)

The warriors, displaying their skill in training through the fourfold methods of weapons and so forth— distinguished by non-attachment, excellence, and agility— struck with both discharged and retained missiles.
Driven by the onset of rage, two others rushed headlong toward their opponent with great speed;
casting aside their weapons like wrestlers, they struck with blows of the fist and engaged in a wrestling match limb-to-limb.
Pure, having incurred no attachment, and released from afar, displaying their swiftness,
those arrows entered the inner army of the enemies and performed what was fitting for their flight.
Having stepped upon the foremost shoulder of the bull and then ascended high onto its head without hesitation,
those possessed of great pride, moving with effortless grace along a superhuman path, ascended easily to heaven.

Some, pervading the space between heaven and earth with their restless limbs that delighted within the body, attained a heavy seat in the assembly and purchased fame at the price of their very lives. (MSV 18.15)

Having performed a heroic deed at the front of the battle, praiseworthy in its energy and valor, those naked ones loudly proclaimed their illustrious names— names that were appropriate for those who are proud yet now ashamed before their enemies, and which had previously been unknown to them.
Charging headlong toward one another, others—
blinded by their own fury— thrust the sharp blades of their swords into the lotus-bosoms of their adversaries with their very chests.
When those two armies had become intermingled, this distinction was generally clear:
those who were turned away from the front were one's own, while he who was facing forward was the enemy. (MSV 18.18)

Because it was of noble lineage, the sword—having been brought into close contact with his limbs and bound to him with great respect—was led by the hand and, having deceived him, committed treachery against someone. (MSV 18.19)
When the armor of one [warrior] was split by the enemy, who resembled a rain-cloud due to the impact of his polished blade,
the path of that sharp-edged weapon— gleaming like lightning— was visible upon the blood-streaked surface of the armor.

With his arm sewn from the tip to the root by means of a long arrow, and with his fist clenched like a frog, he endured unbearable pain; yet, due to his steadfastness, the leather did not slip from his hand, nor from that of anyone else.
Having pierced his nose with an iron hook and being struck on the back of his neck with a vulture-feathered shaft,
Durmukha was unable to open his mouth, even though he was foul-mouthed, as if bound by a tight rope for the sake of training.
The noble steed did not tremble before the elephants intended to strike at him with lances held aloft by their riders;
for do those of noble birth ever cause shame to their masters who desire to perform great deeds for the sake of fame?

Though mounted on elephants and seeking mountain fastnesses as if they were inaccessible fortresses, those victorious warriors— whose nets of arrows reached down to the lower world— were unable to conquer him with their armies, for they were themselves devoid of fear and rendered powerless by his weapons.

Scattering the waves of his army in all directions, he wandered alone, desiring to see his beloved kinsman who had gone far away; like the divine Boar seeking the earth within the ocean, he roamed about.
As long as the elephant driver, knowing how to rouse the rutting spirit, had not applied collyrium to the temples to awaken it,
so long did thick streams of ichor flow from the elephants of their own accord at the mere sound of the army’s roar.
Enraged at another elephant from its scent, and having disregarded its rider by shaking its head,
the elephant, making all directions resound with its terrible roar, threw off its own saddle-cloth.
When his rival elephant drew near, the [king’s] elephant— though its face-covering had been removed,
was overcome by rage, and its cruel eyes were dilated— could not see anything at all, being blinded by intoxication.
Before the Niṣāda woman could quickly remove the elephant’s eye-covering garment,
he was pierced by volleys of arrows from other elephants mounted by their riders, which struck like a flight of herons.
The careless driver of the elephant, facing his enemy, failed to remove the blindfold from the beast’s eyes;
thus, in an instant, the elephant—broken by the heavy weight of its own tusks and blinded by the falling dust—fell upon the king.

Guarding it with effort because of its secure state, another person, having determined that it was indestructible, resolved in his cultivated mind to employ it for a purpose suitable for the time of his final state— whether for his desired passion or for wealth in times of distress.
Touching one another’s temples with their trunks, their tails raised high,
they fought together with their heads turned upward, meeting at the edges and producing the clear sound of clashing tusks.
The teeth of the elephants—longer, closely set, firm, beautifully pointed, and never losing their sharpness—though struck by opposing tusks, did not break; indeed, they themselves were not broken.
The fire produced by the clashing tusks of the elephants, its flickering tips resembling the luster of cut gold,
was not at all noticed by the troops even though it had caught the fly-whisks dyed deep crimson.

In the sky above their lofty heads, the garlands of stars appeared like the fires at the end of an aeon, arising from the friction of the trees that were their tusks as they were embraced by the fierce, uprooting winds of intoxication.
In the herd of horses, dark as thick clouds, their tusks attained a crimson hue from the blood;
they gained such splendor as coral sprouts emerging from the waters of the ocean.
With their banners trembling at their tips, the elephants advanced in a clash, letting out loud, drawn-out cries from their uplifted necks;
plunging deeply into the bodies of other elephants, they tore at their tusks in agony.
Lifting high with his two tusks the enemy elephant that was quivering [in pain],
the one with tusks like ivory pillars clearly attained the likeness of a mountain whose rain-clouds are impaled upon its peaks.
Even when his goad was broken, the elephant, turning his body back and discharging arrows out of shame before the warrior,
repeatedly resisted [the enemy] while being tormented by the constant joy of his driver.
Pervaded by worlds from which it is difficult to escape,
the steadfast and majestic one entered the midst of the army with impetuousness, just as Brahmā, the primordial god, formerly entered the interior of the Primeval Egg.
With his body pierced all over by dense clusters of iron arrows that shone dark like swarms of bees, the elephant,
his desire unshaken in battle due to his fearlessness, gleamed as if his hair stood on end with joy.
As the arrow was swiftly drawn from the corner of his eye by the one standing before him,
a stream of ichor flowing from the elephant king appeared, alas, like a stream of blood from one possessed by wrath.
As the elephants, out of recklessness, were trampling the poles of their tusks upon the surface of the bed of Death,
I immediately suspected from my troops that they had already ascended halfway up the steep path to heaven.

Resembling droplets of moonlight, the mass of pearls leaping forth from the frontal globes of elephants split by sword-strokes shone as if the sky were filled with the essence of a multitude of stars.

The king of elephants, filled with rage, trampled with his foot upon his own severed trunk— which had been cut off by a swiftly hurled discus thrown from afar— and which was writhing violently on the ground, crushing it into a mire of blood.
As the elephant’s body was severed at the fetter and he fell face-down toward the ground without support,
his own pair of tusks, having gained their full length, served as his prop.
Having felt the touch [of the serpent's fangs] from the wound in the earth, he remained for a moment without pain within the space between the elephant's tusks;
then, having conquered the elephant whose gums were severed by the upper half of his sword, he immediately rose up by another way.
Seizing a certain fearless man by the hand before him, a serpent hurled him high into the air;
surely it was for that very reason that he was delivered into the presence of the celestial women seated in the sky.
A certain elephant, its internal stream wounded by a long and very firm spear thrust from afar,
lacked the power to seize with its trunk-tip even that which was right before it.

The divine form of the slender woman, the daughter of Nanda and Gopa, who had been crushed by Kaṃsa as if by an elephant, was seen rising into the sky by those standing on the ground, like Caṇḍikā, while they looked on in amazement.
Having stepped upon one shank with the tip of his forefoot and lifting the other high with his trunk,
that elephant of terrible nature, standing as motionless as a log, tore another through the middle like wood.
The noble one grieved first for his two servants who were fated for death; he did not feel such love for his beloved as he felt for them.
Having previously shown favor to the other and not to the second, he experienced an inner burning due to his subsequent remorse.
When the other’s face was severed from afar by a leaping crescent-moon arrow, his teeth biting his lip in rage,
the army trembled once more at the leaping headless trunk, sword in hand, which had vanished from their sight only to reappear as it was cut at the neck.

Amidst the sounds of musical instruments accompanied by rapid rhythmic beats, as the Kāhalā women sang shrilly and performed dances with hand-gestures devoid of visual focus, the conch shell on his body laughed loudly, resonating within his chest.

When his own army had turned back and was being shattered, some enemies simultaneously showered him with gold-feathered arrows released in a single torrent; yet both sides also showered him with flower garlands and cries of "Well done! like perfected beings.

He remembered the elephants as they wandered frenziedly upon the battlefield, their riders having been struck down by arrows and their seats now empty, while they were being pursued by enemy forces and trampled by other elephants in turn.
Intoxicated by the repeated scent of blood, the lordly elephant, trampling the world upon the earth of the battlefield,
dragged out the long garland clinging to his foot— a garland resembling the noose of Varuṇa.

A certain celestial maiden, having fallen into a swoon after being struck deeply, was sprinkled with the cool spray from the elephant's trunk; wishing to seize him as he began to breathe again, she fainted once more, her purpose rendered futile.

She trembled at the moon-like faces of the Apsarases— simple yet fierce in appearance, resembling Rāhu— as they were about to leap from the mouths of others, whose necks had been severed by arrows and who were soaring high into the sky.

Embracing her hero who had performed well in battle, a certain wife went quickly to a grove on Mount Meru to sport; she did not cast her body into the fire until that very moment, being unable to endure separation from him.
Seeing him who had given up his life in battle while mounted on a female elephant, a certain woman— whose vital breaths had risen at that very moment out of love for him—
attained the unbroken state of divinity through her chastity and embraced him herself.
A certain divine lady, who causes one to dwell in heaven for a long time and maintains her freshness day after day,
was enjoyed by someone in the other world, while she gratifies the people here with her fame.
Surely the inner self of those who had fainted went to the delightful abode of the gods;
for having regained consciousness and witnessed further proof, they exert themselves even more resolutely for battle.

Another, bewildered by the falling of weapons, having regained consciousness after being carried away, turned back from the battle despite his friend's loud cries; he abandoned his life—what indeed is conformity to worldly custom?
Two others, whose chests were pierced by an enemy who drew them from afar because they were nearby,
ascended to heaven while still upright, through the power of their mutual support.

Preventing their own faction from being eager to slay with weapons those high-born men who were deluded and divided, others caused them to be captured alive; for by what person would such worthy objects not be seized? (MSV 18.66)
The parasols, with their broken shafts, lay scattered upon the ground like silver platters of great lunar brilliance set out as an offering for the King of the Dead.
The pearl necklaces of the lifeless kings, marked with saffron and fallen from their chests, shone forth;
I imagine them to be the yellow-and-red teeth of Death, who has attained his full desire, as he drinks the wine of blood.
The blood of those wounded by weapons, which had flowed from the low ground to the high and shone upon the earth—
was that perhaps safflower-dyed water for the purpose of coloring the garments within the inner apartments of Death?
In that battle, Rāma performed a marvel by means of the weapons of the Kṣatriyas, creating five lakes from the blood of his enemies twenty-one times;
at that very moment, countless rivers with islands flowed forth from them.
Severed below the fetters by those who were trained in the three weapons, their bodies sliced by hundreds of sharp blades,
the elephants reached the likeness of tortoises within the rivers of blood flowing from their feet.
Rivers of blood flowed with their equipment intact, as swans in the form of yak-tail whisks— fallen from the ears of elephants— floated upon the waves that surged ever higher.
The leaf-borne vehicles of those who had departed for the sake of the flesh moved upward into the sky;
surely their vital breaths, having been forced to abandon the body by cruel weapons, were even now looking back with longing.
Spreading through the quarters with the whirring of their feathered tips, those sharp arrows reached from afar with their swift, pointed fronts;
first, the blood of the lifeless soldiers was drunk by the living birds, and afterwards, it was consumed by the flocks of arrows themselves.

Surely, the blazing tongue of fire, vomiting forth its bright luster from within under the guise of flames, shrieked aloud as it surely seized the intense vital energy along with the bodies of those endowed with vigor who stood firm in battle.

With the intervals between their bodies severed by a continuous stream of fire, the jackals consumed the flesh of the warriors impaled on arrows— flesh made savory by a unique flavor resulting from the cooking process— using the flames of the fire fed by the fat of those difficult to devour.
Having drunk blood as a medicinal elixir to dispel his illness and awaken from hunger, and having dried up the remnants of his indigestion,
the jackal made a delicious meal of human flesh with the liver as a side dish, devouring the corpse with loud and terrifying cries.

The lotuses of the crocodiles were torn open by swarms of flesh-eating creatures in their hope for fat; surely Time, perceiving that living beings had become despondent, fashioned these terrifying mouths.

Strewn on all sides with the lifeless bodies of living beings, that battlefield shone like the workshop of the Creator at the conclusion of his work of creation, filled with many forms— some fully formed, others half-completed.

As the royal armies approached with unceasing speed, there occurred a tumultuous battle of the haughty forces against the surging hosts of the Lord of Fortune, like the repeated and thunderous clashing of the waves of the great ocean against the currents of the rivers.
Then, in the forest of battle,
he rose up like a fire produced by the friction of a multitude of trees— the kings— being split apart by his arrows, which were like bamboo-sticks.
Displaying his prowess from afar as the elephant charged toward him,
Bala gazed upon it like a lion at a wild elephant.
Then Jaja, Jojauja, Jiji, and Jājī struck him from there;
Bhābha, Abhībhā, Bhibhū, Bhārāri, Ari, and Rīra were his enemies.
Causing the earth to tremble for the sake of the world's continued existence,
his chariot fell like a thunderclap, terrifying with its roar.
Then, O great archer, that skilled warrior, out of anger, loosed sharp arrows at Rāma,
who was himself a great archer and expert in battle.
Like the sun fallen toward the southern quarter,
the charioteer quickly bore him away from the sky before he had lost his strength.
Having subdued the powerful army of Śālva belonging to Śini, that majestic host,
possessing the luster of blooming lotuses, uttered a mighty speech from its mouths.
Having reached the tree with its wealth of leaves shriveled by the firebrand,
it blazed forth with majesty, scattering its brilliance in all directions.
With that very same speech by which he had cast aside his heart's gold and raised his weapon, the bow-armed Rukmī requested the departure [of Pṛthu].
The son of Kṛṣṇa alone received the armies of the kings, which were rushing from all sides simultaneously, just as the ocean receives the rivers.
There, by means of those gleaming iron fangs that bore a resemblance to clouds,
the thunderbolt of arrows was created, possessing the brilliant luster of gold.
Scattered with the blossoms of his fingernails’ rays, he shone like a lofty tree, upon whose branches of trembling bows rested bees in the form of arrows.
Having encountered that terrible battle,
he, who possessed kindness even toward those who bowed down and was the destroyer of hosts of enemies, did not release his arrows at them.
Before him, Kṛta shattered with his arrows the many shafts of Bāṇa, who stood there with the hope of victory over all the kings.
While the army, having employed many stratagems, was advancing with force, he,
drawing his bow, advanced toward it without effort or stratagem.
Having instantly surpassed Uttamaujas in vigor and great energy,
he humbled him and established himself as the preeminent leader in the assembly.
From afar alone, Kumāra struck down those armies with his broad-headed arrows;
he did not strike them again in close combat, for they were already filled with awe.
Having been swiftly crushed by him and released with utter indifference,
his enemies— unlike arrows— fell into a state of utter embarrassment.
In that battle, the gods stationed in the sky, along with the great ṛṣis, suddenly praised his prowess with hair-raising tales of his heroic deeds.
A profusion of white, unfading flowers fell from the sky, perfuming the quarters;
from that, his fame soared up to heaven.
The enemies were unable to withstand him in battle, for he was one who warded off the onset of age; and he overspread the heavens with his fame, which likewise warded off the clouds.
The head of the battle, filled with a multitude of hair-like soldiers, was adorned by the blossoming flower-marked [sun] as if by a crest-ornament.
Although she fought with great respect for him, that army— lacking respect for any other man—
was led into a state of fear as it retreated, driven by its passion for him.
Seeing the fish-bannered god thus embraced by the Goddess of Victory as if she were enraged,
the King of Cedi was instantly seized by fury.
Accompanied by his fourfold army, which bore along with it what was not beneficial,
the proud king set forth, while his fourfold host resembled playful young elephants.
Then, by the expansive sounds of the twanging of that bow’s string,
it resembled the oceans agitated at the end of an eon by the sounding of musical instruments.
With causes, various forms, bodies, and weapons;
with tastes, sounds, vehicles, and essences; with sounds, words, and musical instruments.
The sister of Yama herself, dark as a mass of swaying black serpents, desired to provide assistance, appearing as if clad in shimmering iron armor.
At the start of his arrival, she sat down with longing, intoxicated by the sound of his high-pitched cry; she was free from the illness of not seeing the steady one arrive.
Those who were foremost among the kings, whose intentions were purified by ascetic virtues, stood firm; for that was the time when the touchstone of the courage and loyalty of servants was revealed.
Who, bearing a sword-blade that possessed a soft and stainless luster, was able to ascend to heaven with his weapon, possessing a stainless and pure excellence? (MSpv 19.31)
The soldiers, having simultaneously generated great force,
sought to overcome their opponents with their club-like arms and their shanks against one another.
Then, from the pride of the mounts,
there arose a sound like the trumpeting of rutting, powerful, and noble elephants, a roar like the crashing of a heavy thunderbolt.
The army, carrying away the sound of its rapid movement, attained the highest state through the essence of passion;
it was a mass of extended men and arrows, a battle for those who honor their own people.
The bow-creepers, whose middles were graspable by the fist, though drawn forcibly by those arrogant in youth, cried out loudly as their integrity remained unbroken.
The many elephants in rut produced dust, and there were thousands of bells;
from the elephants came a spray of water, and by that, the dust was laid to rest.
Even though the elephants were colored with the fresh dye of the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*),
in that battle, they manifested only the fierce sentiment (*raudra-rasa*) through their furious agitation.

He did not waver from his master regarding those who had attained mental resolve, nor did he feel fear toward those who, having encountered him in the singular onset of battle, were intent on their own mental resolve.
The forest of battle became terrifying with its tree-like archers, whose hollows were quivers filled to the brim with arrows, and whose arms were like branches embraced by leathern finger-guards.
Disregarding various kinds of rebukes, she, possessing the dense power of a flood of people and endowed with vastness, suffered a supreme loss here.
With its various arrays— such as the *viṣama*, *sarvatobhadra*, *cakra*, and *gomūtrikā*—
that army became like a great epic poem composed of verses.
Having united with the Sātvatas, he marched forth with a brilliant army against the King of Cedi to fight,
an army that had attained its full splendor through its own inherent power.
Broad, deep, and filled with restless people,
the army of the enemies fell upon the royal road like a carriage track.
That army— deep as a lordly elephant, resounding with the cries of brave hosts, having brought about the slaughter of enemies, irresistible, and warding off foes— was [deployed].
Swift and life-taking arrows, resembling peacocks with their beautiful, spreading plumage,
fell in abundance like great serpents.
While the battle was underway, those who were not devoid of courage showered expanding gifts even upon their opponents;
likewise, even those with horns engaged in combat while showering expanding gifts.

The battle was illuminated by foot soldiers who had been deployed in front, who were in motion, and who had attained purity, just as the art of music (*gāndharva*) is illuminated by words that are uttered first, set in motion, and refined.
By a certain attendant, the faultlessness of others at the head of the assembly was attained;
the faultlessness of the earth’s surface, pervaded by fame, was reached.
To strike down his enemies, someone simultaneously drew both his sharp sword and himself away from his closely knit retinue.
Another, a lover of excessive luxury, brandished his weapon excessively;
by that one who was exceedingly unrestrained, the army was swiftly struck down.
A certain enemy, completing his thousandth count, had his head severed by a sword;
thus, even while still upright, he underwent the performance of a dance like that of a headless trunk.
Adorned with the beautiful ornaments of wounds from weapons,
another was seen, adorned with ornaments like Rāvaṇa.
Another, whose pair of thighs had been cast down by the cutting and cleaving of his enemies,
became red-bodied in both ways, being sprinkled with weapons.
In that great battle, another assumed a terrifying form like the ocean;
his wrath increased in the great conflict, like the anger of Śiva toward Dakṣa.
In their fury, the foot soldiers— whose swords had been severed by the enemy’s blades— bit their own teeth like elephants attacking a rival.
In that battle, which was characterized by the skillful rending of elephants with impetuous force,
there was no one who did not feel fear as they were torn apart.
As long as those desiring to discharge their debt of affection toward their master did not honor him, others,
out of indignation, abandoned their lives in battle.
In this world difficult to look upon because of infamy, there is no abode for anger except death;
in this world difficult to look upon because of infamy, there is no abiding in anger except through death.
Though it faltered due to his mental sharpness, the spear—possessing its supreme power—was released; yet it was the iron spear that failed, not the one born of his body.
The kings engaged in battle with their armies;
thus did the divine army cause wonder among the people.
Like courtesans who attract lovers with their own virtues until the fruit is attained, those three-edged arrows suddenly released their shafts.
The swift horses of the enemy army, having begun their gallop,
and the arrows with their rapid flight, entered into the midst of them.

Having placed the fruit at the forefront, those who were renowned for their reliance on the side of the virtuous quickly attained the target with their arrows, which had been well-feathered by their practice.
One man, having pierced his enemies before him with arrows whose color was like the *japā* flower, caused them to discharge blood that possessed a hue equal to that of the flower.
As the two, desiring battle, approached from afar with speed toward the powerful one,
the elephant between them became lifeless like a mere wooden barricade.
The female elephants,
fearless and resembling clouds, trumpeted loudly with their bellows, while the male elephants— vast, heavy, formidable, and capable of bearing the burden of the earth— roared in response.
Elephants, while fighting, did not attain such helplessness from their trunks being severed by sharp sword-blades as they did from their tusks being broken.
As if crushed by one another,
the bodies of those beings who had fallen into a state of mercilessness flowed with the water of their tears incessantly on all sides.
The elephant, like a lotus-pond on the field of battle drenched with the waters of rut,
churned about the hundred-petaled lotuses drawn up by its broad trunk.
When the elephant was wounded by arrows and was sinking deeply in despair as if from poison, the bees there seemed to weep under the pretext of their humming.
On that vast battlefield, which was like the bed of Death himself, the great elephants assumed the state of bedbugs due to the calamity of their tusks being bitten off.
Who indeed could delight in this, which destroys the joy of the terrified,
while the army of Kāma shines forth, making even the slow-witted one desire passion?
Even while repeatedly manifesting a terrible demonic disposition in battle,
those who were slain by their enemies while facing them attained the state of gods.
Because the immortals, with their arrows, struck his limbs as if they were wounds,
he attained equality with the immortals by means of his sword and its sheath.
With friends, masters, paternal uncles, brothers, and maternal uncles struck down,
that battlefield was beheld by the steadfast as if it were the grammar of Pāṇini.
When the dust was raised by the Indus, whose waters of blood resembled the clouds of twilight,
the people who had gone out to fight became as if delighted with their eyes in that blood-stained dust.
Strewn with bursting lotuses, crowded with falling shells, filled with swimming birds,
and possessing red lotuses for their water-born flowers, the rivers flowed forth.
The blood-drinking man, who destroys the pride of men and consumes marrow and fat,
rejoiced in the destruction of the fresh marrow and fat of the Rākṣasas and Piśācas.
With their bowstrings removed, their bows appeared variegated and their hearts quivering with blood;
that display of the heroes shone like a mass of clouds with lightning.
When his kinsman had perished, many men here in his presence lamented; yet in that army, no one wailed when the bell near the slain man fell silent.
The earth, strewn with the severed tusks and limbs of elephants,
shone like the world of mortals covered by the pestles and mortars of Death, which had crushed the lives of beings.
Having thus shaken off other men in battle,
the King of Cedi advanced against his enemies and, through his assault, utterly defeated those men.
Then [he appeared] with his yellow garment dappled by the reflections of the gems upon his chest, like a cloud accompanied by lightning that is streaked by a shimmering rainbow.
He was dark-hued, resting upon a blue lotus with its stalk;
he was surrounded by bees that hovered about him; he was sufficient for the dalliance of women; he was playful and fond of sport; and he was one who cherished his followers.
O King, with her body seen as if she were someone new, filled with longing for union at that very moment, she was like the Goddess of Victory herself with her side-long glances.
The discerning one, the powerful one, the radiant one, the one whose radiance has ceased, the one who has transcended, the fearless one;
the conqueror of existence, the one who has cast off becoming, the non-existence of becoming, the pervasive lord of the world.
By those supreme yogins who were determined to reach the further shore, who desired to attain it,
and who were intent on casting off their bodies, the Supreme Person was beheld.
He was resorted to by that daughter of noble birth, who was endowed with dense splendor, radiant luster, and that very essence;
she was swift-moving, beautiful-breasted, and faultless.
Even though their enemies looked upon them with hostility, they remained free from sin;
for medicine is by its very nature a destroyer of disease, even if it is unpleasant to the taste.
"O you who are known in heaven, go to those armies in the conquered field;
O you who are free from disease, may there be no obstructors against the cow, for he is our warrior who bows not to us."
When he was being appointed to a most weighty task before him,
he bent the bow as his lord placed the great string upon it.
There, arrows were fitted that were both very harsh and beautiful;
when drawn by him, they became very harsh to his enemies yet beautiful to behold.
Even among those men who had been left behind, like arrows that had missed their mark,
whoever was endowed with merit reached as far as Karna's ear.
On the bank of the river, the enemy of the enemy, the supreme one, filled with form and fullness, was further filled by others;
and even above, he was filled from the front by others who were boundless and free from blemish.
In a single instant, he discharged sharp, piercing arrows that reached the very horizon, dripping with venom and capable of cleaving the vital organs, against his enemies.
Raining arrows, emitting a great roar, with his bow and banner quivering,
he of dark-blue complexion shone like a cloud in the guise of Keśava.
Not only did people behold his bow, which was drawn into a circle, but even the enemies perceived the power of that one who acts with swift precision.
He is the illuminator of the world, free from passion and untainted by impurity;
he has hair like a swarm of bees, he is Time itself, yet partless and beyond strife. Indeed, at the end of time, he is intent upon the sport of the boar.
He pierced his armored enemies in their unblinking pupils;
for in him, the mark was never wide of the aim except when it came to the distribution of gifts.
The hero, the bestower of boons, who is without flaw, who dispels his enemies, and whose roar is like the sound of water,
destroyed the enmity— just as the sun destroys barren soil.
Having released many arrows that took the lives of most of his enemies,
his bow could not endure the vitality of any other [bow].
The king of kings, the ageless, the stainless, the unborn, the unconquered, shone upon the courtyard of the enemy's field;
he, the conqueror of foes, the destroyer of the strength of his enemies, the crusher of the wicked, shone with a splendor that was never worn away.
As he, the haughty one, was slaying his enemies, his arrows went toward two things:
to blood for the purpose of drinking, and to the world for the purpose of protection.
The crusher of cruel enemies, the bringer of prosperity, the performer of deeds, the one whose hands are like flower-buds, the young shoot, the one who destroys the hard and the wicked. (MSpv 19.104)
Although he had descended to the earth to lighten its burden,
he created a multitude of enemies that increased the earth's weight.
He who destroys poverty, who is a destroyer of enemies, who is a giver of garments,
who has no fear from afar, who is free from cruelty, who is not consumed by distress, who is a destroyer of the womb of the earth, who is a giver of great wealth, and who is full of reverence.
Piercing his enemies gathered in a multitude with a single arrow as if they were trees,
he acted in a manner consistent with himself, who had found delight in a previous birth.
The heroic Śauri,
the lord of the body of Śrī, the destroyer of hosts, the slayer of enemies, swiftly pierced the heads of his foes with arrows that were not cold and reached to the ends of the quarters.
Because he had spoken thus, the arrows discharged repeatedly by those whose enemies were their foes did not even leave a mark upon their hearts, though they struck their bodies.
Therefore, so that there might be no defilement of his master’s name and syllables, the arrows did not take up a garland made of the life-breaths of other men's wives. MSpv 19.110.
Having snatched away the very life-essence of the host of warriors with their swift arrows, they vanished from sight in the distance like thieves upon the earth.
The Conqueror (Jina) made the earth drenched in blood from that army, which possessed a king of terrible weapons, a king of banners, and who had donned fearsome armor.
The enemy force was pervaded by birds whose beaks were suited for piercing flesh, while his own arrows filled the sky with their activity-less emptiness.
Giver upon giver, giver of the giver of givers, giver of the giver of the giver;
giver of the giver of the giver of the giver, giver of the giver of the giver of the giver; giver of the giver of the giver of the giver of the giver, you have given that which was not given.

With streams of blood flowing from the wounds in the hearts of his enemies— blood that issued from the frontal globes of elephants and their breasts— he set in motion rivers of gore for both his foes and their wives.
Abounding in the strength of one ever-subdued, with his vital energy fully aroused, the illustrious Hāri, whose prowess was well-known, shone like another Hari.
Though he was but one, his enemies, seeing him as twofold, threefold, and fourfold through their rivalry,
immediately met their own destruction.
Always possessing a body perfected by fortune in battles where the filling of [desires] was divinely accomplished, he,
the great one, attained an exceedingly vast majesty that was like the shore of the great ocean.
Having accomplished their purpose for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, these feathered arrows quickly enter the earth with downward faces;
this indeed is fitting for those who, though pure, have been cast into the midst of the enemy host by their master.

Then, having seized that noble being who was distinguished by his courage with the impetuosity of battle, the fortunate one—having attained purity through the destruction of his sins, the ground of whose chest bore the most exalted *śrīvatsa* mark, and who was free from fear like the supreme hunter of deer—joyfully released a lion’s roar. Simultaneously with that roar, he covered the sky with floods of arrows that rose up like clouds.
Bearing a face with three furrowed lines shining brightly and made terrifying by a pair of high, knitted brows,
the King of Cedi, showing no fear, challenged the Murāri to battle while disregarding his prowess.
As he bore upon his shoulders a death that awaited him like the falling of a sharp-edged wheel,
the chariot, its horses urged on, sped toward Śauri by means of destiny appearing in the form of a charioteer.

The chariot of Śauri also descended to the earth, staining the ground with the blood flowing from the body of Aśvasena, who had been crushed by the heavy rim of the wheel and whose body was as red as Jāguḍa and saffron.
With the ends of his banner-cloth streaming out, its small bells tinkling with a sweet sound,
he shone like Death himself with loosened hair, made resonant by his vow to destroy his enemies.
The sound of the chariot, filling the quarters of the sky and imitating the roar of water-laden clouds,
was heard by the blue-necked peacocks who raised their necks and spread their plumage.
Beholding upon the chest of Acyuta the mark of saffron from the breasts of the daughter of the King of Vidarbha,
the King of Cedi, though he had long served him, was suddenly seized by rage and immediately entered into a state of union with death.
The king drew his bow high, its twanging sound evoking the fear of a thunderclap;
its string quivered like the crest of the fire at the end of an aeon, fanned by the restless winds.
Then, with arrows that were clearly characterized by simultaneous drawing, aiming,
pulling back, and release, that impetuous warrior rained down a shower of shafts to overwhelm Upendra.
For those arrows that possessed the purity of being endowed with the fruit of straightness and took refuge in the faction of the teacher,
a fitting alliance was formed with the bow once they had become curved through their possession of virtue.

When the King of Cedi, who had mastered his senses, performed a feat upon that most unbearable bow, the string rang out loudly as its life-force trembled from being forcibly drawn with such intense pain.
Then, like words issuing from the mouth of a debater— possessing continuity, clarity, purity, and adhering to their respective positions— the arrows of the king’s bow flew forth.
People beheld his bow, possessing the dark luster of a buffalo's horn, with its terrible, long staff-like arms positioned at its center,
appearing as fearsome in form as the enraged God of Death with his pair of upraised eyebrows.

The sky was covered by volleys of arrows that possessed shafts of gold as brilliant as lightning, with iron-tipped heads dark as clouds, resounding as they flew with great speed and gathered in dense masses like rain-clouds descending with force.

The arrows with golden shafts, from which water flowed like clouds split by the tips of cold spears, spread across the circle of the quarters as if they were streams of tears flowing from those suffering intense pain.

As he departed, the earth—its splendor obscured by clouds and its light veiled by mist—was momentarily unpleasant to the people, whether they were on the path of vision or in the sky; it was held back as if by his steady arrows, having fallen away from its natural state.
The king constructed a vast shelter made of a network of arrows on all sides, which shielded the entire army of the enemy of Mura from the heat of the sun, as if it were a single great mansion.
When the king spoke thus, the army of the slayer of Danu’s sons was then hemmed in on all sides by that host of mountains,
like a wheel brought to a standstill within the cage of a bird-net.
Then that single hero, the Unshakable One, neutralized with his own arrows the manifold rain of shafts discharged by his enemy;
or rather, he refuted the proofs established by his opponents with his own proofs, like a respondent refuting an opponent.
With his elbow bent and drawing the bowstring toward his ear, that bow resounded loudly, imitating the cry of a rutting krauñca bird at the edge of a dense forest.
With his chest expanded and his shoulders cast down, his head curved like that of a peacock,
he then shone as if momentarily carved by a master’s skill, his fists held steady from beginning to end.
From his bow, countless arrows— heavy, shaped like flashes of lightning, and possessing swift-moving strings— fell rapidly with a great roar, like clouds falling from a mass of clouds.
With his high-peaked and rugged shoulder-blade covering one quarter of the horizon with its vast expanse,
this single arm of his, when once extended, was gazed upon by the armies like a sovereign mountain.
The arrows of him whose banner bears the eagle, with their tips unblunted, brought that volley of shafts discharged by the enemy to pieces—
just as those of improper character bring about the ruin of a king who leads his subjects astray.
As if rejected by her beloved, the volley of the enemy’s arrows— bright with their glowing shaft-marks—
fell fruitlessly to the earth, having become lightened as they were struck head-on by the arrows of Murāri.
And the messengers, struck violently in front by the Vatsa horses released by Mādhava,
retreated like cowards in the opposite direction from the earth that had become completely full.
Born from the mutual friction [of the clouds], with sparks scattered by the clashing of their throats,
the fire momentarily blazes among other masses of clouds as it licks at their layers.
When the cloud-mass of the enemy’s arrows was dispersed by the Lord, as the beauty of autumn disperses the clouds,
the Yādava armies— with their lotus-faces blooming— shone intensely like the quarters of the sky.
He covered the sky with floods of arrows that rendered the orb of the sun's brilliance a mere pretense;
yet, to the people, only a single deer appeared to have been released at once from his bow-staff.
For even a well-wisher who has come clearly from the enemy side is not a bringer of peace;
thus, the flood of javelins released by Kṛṣṇa caused Śiśupāla’s forces to suffer all the more.
With their golden-brown brilliance, the arrows, whizzing with a fierce and rapid sound through their feathers,
entered the surface of the earth like the sons of Vinatā, causing the serpents to writhe in agitation and confusion.
Hundreds of harsh, sharp arrows were discharged by Śiśupāla from his city;
though they pierced the vital organs, they caused no pain to the enemy of the Dānavas, just as offenses do not cause distress to one who has transcended all faults.

When the Lord of the Murus desired to destroy the world by means of his illusory power— having already manifested the marvelous illusion of creating the universe— the king employed the "Sleep" weapon, which is the very sleep of cosmic dissolution at the end of time.
Dark as the body of a boar wet with water, rendering the sun a name devoid of meaning,
that darkness made the lotus-like eyes of his army close in sleep.
That even the teachers and the lords of the earth fell asleep while seated upon their bows is not to be wondered at;
for even though they were constantly awake to ward off calamity, they remained seated right there.
Likewise, as others fell into lassitude and abandoned their own power to maintain [the teachings],
the weapon slipped from their foremost hands— just as a scripture, though well-learned, slips from the hands of those possessed by passion.
Although he was accustomed to sleeping upon the mass of waters, while remaining in the midst of his own ocean of power,
that Supreme Person alone remained awake there, ever vigilant for the sake of the three worlds.
Then, as his gaze fell upon the mirror-like Kaustubha gem, it was as if the brilliance of the sun had arisen;
yet that radiance was not surprising, for he is indeed the All-pervading Lord whose eyes are the moon and the sun.

Like the favor shown by a great man toward those who bow before him, that mass of light from the jewel at the tip of his crest spread forth, bestowing unclouded vision upon the troops whose eyes were wide open.

And with feet restored to their natural state, the world of living beings was able once more to move about; casting off the stupor caused by the overwhelming darkness, they immediately regained their vitality.
Since the enemies were repeatedly overcome in battle by the Yadu warriors with their speed despite thick darkness,
surely the lord of light shines all the more brightly when released from the obstruction of clouds.
Then, when the darkness had been conquered by the light— just as a legal proceeding dispels a false accusation—
he recited the spell that is the mother of serpents possessing fierce and terrifying coils.
Then, the lords of serpents, bearing broad hoods and incessantly vomiting venom from their mouths,
became visible with both corners of their lips licked by pairs of flickering tongues all at once.
By the sons of Kadrū, who through deceit desired victory in the sky at that very moment by means of their artificial transformation of hair,
the tail of the Lord of the Mare was seized, just as in former times it had been seized in the city of the drinkers of the first draught of nectar.
Assuming their full stature through ancient honor, the broad regions shone forth, possessing fame as vast as eyes;
they were like the elaborate scenes of a drama, whose acts are composed by poets skilled in the Bharata tradition.
The body of the serpents, its rays dimmed by the thick smoke rising from their venomous breath,
assumed the luster of a coppery orb, as if the sun were eclipsed.
With their coils coiling about in apprehension at the sight of the crest-ornaments made of peacock feathers on the banners,
those flickering tongues fell upon the hosts of the Vṛṣṇis like the nooses of Yama for swift binding.
The silken banners upon the bodies of the serpents bore the luster of freshly shed skins, white as the canopy of foam shimmering amidst the circles of waves in the vast ocean.
With the coils of serpents forming a circle around their heads and hanging down across their chests,
the people shone as if they were wearing garlands of blooming blue lotuses.
With their bodies entwined from the roots to the heads by serpents bearing jewel-like flowers,
those men bore the likeness of trees encircled by long climbing vines.
Serpents, possessing the dark luster of thick collyrium paste and mud, slithering here and there over his body,
assumed the graceful appearance of leather girths fastened to the horses' clearly visible saddle-cloths.

The slender body of the great serpent, dark blue as a cloud and spreading impetuously, coiling itself around him at every step, rendered him motionless like an elephant in its stable, owing to its great length.
Then, at the glance of Mādhava, which was accompanied by a smile and the raising of one eyebrow in a gesture of disdain,
tens of thousands of birds— residing upon the head of his own banner, the Suparṇa— flew upward.
The birds, possessing the luster of molten gold, as they flew up from the great roar uttered by the king of birds,
were for a moment gazed upon from on high by the armies like the sparks of a blazing seven-rayed fire.

He attained a likeness to the Garuḍas born of the lineage of the mountains, who sport in the ocean of the sky between Mount Sumeru and the earth, scattering great clouds with their flickering wings like fish.
With its rays flashing all around and turning the quarters of the sky a deep reddish-brown as they fell,
the sun’s orb became exceedingly difficult to behold, like a mirror whose surface is obscured by those very rays.

The serpents bearing their hoods possessed the luster of jewels born from the bile of the lord of snakes, strained out during the churning of the ocean with Mount Mandara as the churning-stick— lusters that were now surpassed by the radiant splendor of the emerging Garuḍas.

The wind, born from the wings of the enemy of the serpents, produced a deep sound like that of the agitated ocean; uprooting multitudes of trees along with their roots, it gave rise to the suspicion that the end of an eon had arrived.

The serpents, overwhelmed by fear and rendered helpless, quickly entered their own abodes by paths cleared by the forceful uprooting of mountains caused by the wind from the wings of the soaring king of birds.

When his own army was brought to destruction by the sky-rangers— who, though acting righteously, behaved like evildoers— against that inexhaustible host, the enemy then, blazing with rage like the fire at the end of an eon, invoked the mantra of the Fire-god.
Then, suddenly assuming the splendor of a violent, loud laugh with a roar that terrified living beings,
Vahni leapt high into the air like a Vetāla, his arms raised aloft with long weapons.
With its banner of smoke stirred and uplifted, its crimson horses ascending swiftly to the sky,
driven by the charioteer of the rapid wind, that fire— beautiful as a golden chariot— set forth.
The fire, with its flames blazing within the hollow of the sky, emitting smoke from the thick, moist clouds as its fuel,
and with long logs of wood set ablaze, consumed the entire universe like a towering tree.
The clouds— white with water dried up by the intense heat, momentarily assuming a coppery glow from the clinging fire,
and turning to soot due to their lack of substance— once again regained their original form.
With their tips flickering like blazing fire and possessing the yellow luster of shimmering gold-leaf,
the banners seemed to attain an exceedingly long duration for a mere moment when all else was non-existent.
Then Murāri, seeing the sky— which he had long rendered like molten gold of exquisite beauty by making it entirely dark—
recalled the fire-weapon *Meghaṅkara*, which is capable of neutralizing [the darkness].

From the hair-tufts of the body of the Three-Fold Abode— which possesses a deep-wombed belly containing the four oceans and into whose joints all rivers have dissolved— there arose wreaths of clouds in the form of water.
Making the *kakubha* trees resound with their cries, spreading across and obscuring the mass of sunlight,
the clouds suddenly surged upward, bringing about a state of deep blackness.
The sky became filled with the thunderous roar of gathering, surging clouds, and the loud laughter of flickering, towering flashes of lightning, white as streaks of refined gold.

With clouds shimmering on all sides, possessing the luster of the rays of the sun and the appearance of the bodies of elephants recently anointed with oil, they seemed to perform the act of bowing down before the fire of destruction.

Roaring like bulls, the clouds rained down water upon the riverbanks; appearing as if they were displaying the deluge at the end of an aeon to extinguish the blazing fire, they drenched the waters that had been brought to the slopes.
At first, he shone even more brightly with sweet and pure waters;
then, like a lover’s anger, he gradually subsided through disputes, as he was a friend of the wind.
Being forcibly driven from all sides by showers of arrows, the fire, seeking its end,
skillfully entered the powerful clouds under the guise of lightning.
In one place, the flame of the fire, its root having been severed, was observed subsiding;
it was like a single feather of the Lord of Birds broken off by the blow of a weapon hurled by Indra.
Having extinguished the masses of fire with their torrents of rain, the clouds suddenly departed from the faces of the quarters;
for the great, having naturally benefited others, do not cause them obstruction.

The sky, scorched by the flames of the blazing fire and repeatedly drenched with fresh water, attained the appearance of a sword that has been heated and then quenched, its surface marred by the wounds inflicted by clouds.
Thus, whatever weapon the king manifested, acting with swift violence like a provoked disease manifesting its transformation,
Murāri, knowing the proper sequence, immediately countered each one in turn with a remedy that cuts away deep-seated evils, like a physician treating a grave malady.

Then his adversary tormented him with the arrows of speech— arrows that were exceedingly crooked, utterly impure, piercing the vital organs, and impossible to withstand, even though he had been conquered by arrows that were supremely straight, pure, and unable to strike his vital points without first dislodging them.
By him who had rendered in vain the beauty of hardness upon the breasts of Rāhu’s wife— breasts that were spoiled by being indulged solely in the sport of tight embraces—
he, the conqueror of Mura, while the demon was still crying out, shattered his body with a discus whose rim was fringed by the flickering flames of the fire of destruction.

Adorned with splendor, accompanied by divine sounds of drums and showers of flowers, and being praised for a moment by hosts of sages, he emerged; then, as his body—which was the very abode of Viṣṇu—cast its radiance into the sky like the rays of the sun, it was beheld by the kings with eyes wide with wonder.
